news.title: New Mexico Republican Rejects Trump’s Push to Rename State
news.text: Gregg Hull, Republican candidate for governor in New Mexico, balked at President Donald Trump's push to rename the state as "New America." In a post to Truth Social earlier on Monday, the president said, "New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" He said the name change would add great "value and prestige," adding that incomes and home values would rise. "Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!" Trump said. Hull responded to the president's idea in a post to X on Monday night, saying in part that he stands by his original statement that "New Mexico does not need a new name." This is not the first time the president has floated the idea. In September, he posted a picture depicting the state with Mexico crossed out and America written below. During his time in office, the president has also rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America. He has also floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait" amid the country's ongoing war with Iran. When reached about Hull's remarks, the White House referred Newsweek to the president's comments. What To Know Hull added in his post on X that the state's identity is rooted in rich culture, beautiful landscape and the resilience of its people. "That identity is never up for negotiation. EVER," Hull said. He added that the people of New Mexico are focused on good-paying jobs, taxes and an economy that works for families, energy independence and relief from rising costs. "That is where my focus is, and that is what the campaign is about," Hull concluded. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump lost New Mexico during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 6 percent. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. Gas prices in New Mexico, meanwhile, are above the national average, according to AAA. On Monday, a gallon of regular gasoline there cost $4.3465 compared to the national average of $4.2953. Last month, an article in the Albuquerque Journal ripped into the president's proposal of renaming the state, calling it, "so elementary and such low-hanging fruit, the biggest surprise was that it took so long for him to make it." In the op-ed by journalist Ryan Boetel he continued, saying, "My advice: Don't waste your breath," he said. "When immature people get frustrated, there's a tried and tired tactic of acting more and more obnoxious to get a rise out of someone to bring them down to their level." MapQuest, which recently defied Trump on his renaming of Lake Ontario, reacted to the moment on X Monday, saying, "Hey, boo. @NewMexico" New Mexico Lawmakers React to Trump's Proposal Senator Ben Ray Lujan, a Democrat, said that New Mexico's name carries history and will remain intact long after Trump is out of office. "New Mexico’s name dates back hundreds of years, long before the United States even existed. It carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are. We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico," Lujan said on X Monday. Democratic Governor Michelle Grisham reacted on X, saying, "This tired New America bit again?" "You have to ask — what policy failure is Trump trying to distract Americans from this time? Let me repeat: New Mexico was New Mexico long before the United States existed and we’ll be New Mexico forevermore," she continued on Monday. "And while we’re talking about our great state, Americans should also know we’ve been busy delivering universal, no cost child care. We’re also the only state that fully replaced health care subsidies that were gutted by Trump and congressional Republicans. Independent experts say our elections are among the most secure in the nation. It’s just that Trump can’t seem to accept that voters are rewarding Democrats for policies that make life easier for working families. ¡Viva Nuevo Mexico!" Newsweek reached out to the Republican Party of New Mexico via email for comment. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: This is not the first time the president has floated the idea of renaming the state "New America."

news.title: Top Dem Strategist Makes Shock Midterms Wish
news.text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville has revealed his surprising take on how he’d like the midterms to pan out.

Carville, 81, told The Bulwark’s Bill Kristol that he would rather see Republicans keep the House majority by five seats than have Democrats take it by the same margin.

“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats,” the former Bill Clinton aide told Kristol on the Bulwark on Sunday podcast. “That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats to win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA.”

Carville was referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, a progressive wing of the Democratic Party that has surged in popularity over the last year and includes populist leaders like New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Carville said that only a slight majority would be difficult for Democratic House leaders, such as Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, to manage.

“Hakeem cannot move. There’s no place to go,” he said. “And even if you have a close Senate, Fetterman would keep Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night.”

“I think this one is one of these races where margin matters a lot,” the politico explained. “Winning big—it’s almost as big as winning, which is weird. But yeah, it’s a nightmare at 225.”

CNN’s Erin Burnett covered Carville’s remarks Monday night, asking former Fox News anchor Gretchen Carlson and former Kamala Harris aide Jamal Simmons their thoughts on his wish.

Carlson said she agreed with the veteran politico about the DSA being “problematic” for the Democratic Party, but disagreed that Democrats would want Republicans to keep the House.

Simmons, on the other hand, said most people in the mainstream Democratic Party don’t share Carville’s hardline views on the DSA.

“While there are lots of issues people may disagree with on the DSA, what they do want is somebody who’s gonna rip up the old playbook and do things differently,” he said. “The American public is interested in doing something really different.”

Carville has made his disdain for the rising democratic socialist coalition clear over the past several months.

After a string of DSA primary victories, such as Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania and Melat Kiros in Colorado, the strategist has unleashed criticism on the progressive splinter group, calling them “a bunch of silly people” and “a pack of fools.”

“Nobody pays attention to them. They don’t do anything,” he told Fox News’s Jesse Watters in August.

In June, he targeted New York DSA candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier directly, saying he doesn’t “have anything in common with someone that says they’re against interracial dating or doesn’t want any incarceration for convicted felons.”

He elevated his rhetoric in August, demanding that DSA candidates quit using the Democratic Party’s “goddamn name.”

news.title: Latino Support for GOP's Byron Donalds in Doubt for Florida Governor's Race
news.text: A new poll shows that Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly overall in the race to be Florida's next governor, but Latinos favor the Democrat by 5 percent. Donalds landed 50 percent overall compared to Jolly's 42 percent, the new N+ Univision/YouGov poll shows on Monday. Among Latinos however, Jolly received 48 percent compared to Donalds' 43 percent. The poll also shows that President Donald Trump's favorability among the key voting bloc is more negative versus the overall with 38 percent favorability compared to a 54 percent unfavorable rating. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. Trump won Florida, his home state, in the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris by double digits. Winning the state was notable amid Trump's broader victory as he made inroads with Hispanic dominant communities and counties in the state like Miami-Dade, Hillsborough and Osceola. Newsweek reached out to both Jolly and Donalds' campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know Florida, once considered a battleground, has shifted to the right over time and is now seen as a reliable pickup for Republicans. An influx of conservative retirees into the state, as well as Trump’s inroads with Latinos, helped turn the state into a stronghold. However, Democrats are hoping to make the state more competitive again in November's midterm with nominee Jolly for governor and Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate leading the top of the ticket. The new poll shows that Cubans favor Trump-endorsed Donalds by 51 percent to 42 percent, Puerto Ricans favor Jolly 51 percent to 35 percent and South Americans prefer Jolly 47 percent to Donalds' 44 percent. Among Latinos who voted for the president in 2024, 9 percent support Jolly, the poll shows. Fifty-five percent of Latinos also say that immigration enforcement has gone too far. That figure combines 32 percent who say the border needed securing, while noting that enforcement has gone too far and an additional 23 percent who say that the border situation was overstated, and enforcement has gone too far, according to the poll. The survey shows that 41 percent of Latinos are very or somewhat concerned that they or someone close to them could be affected by immigration enforcements. Twenty-nine percent of Latino Trump voters also say that immigration enforcement has gone too far, the poll shows. Affordability is a key issue among Sunshine State voters, and 59 percent of Latinos say jobs and the cost of living are a top issue in the state, 57 percent say the cost of housing and affordability while 33 percent say immigration and immigration enforcement. Clarissa Martinez, Vice President of Unidos US, a nonprofit and non-party affiliated organization, told Newsweek via email on Monday, “The poll is consistent with Hispanic voter sentiment in Florida and nationwide: there is widespread discontent with the economy. Hispanic voters have noted that the two top issues shaping Hispanic voters’ views of the President are the cost of living and immigration enforcement, and these are two potent factors swinging these voters away from Republicans.” The poll surveyed 825 Florida voters from October 2 to October 15 and had a margin of error of 4 percent. What Other Polling Shows A Stetson University Center for Public Opinion Research poll shows Donalds up 52 percent to Jolly's 41 percent among likely voters. The survey shows that about 5 percent are undecided and 3 percent would pick another candidate. The poll surveyed 826 Florida adults from October 1 to October 9 and had a 4.2 percent margin of error. A Mason-Dixon Poll for NBC 6 and Telemundo showed Donalds up 48 percent to Jolly's 41 percent overall. One percent said other and 10 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 625 registered voters in the state from September 28 through October 1, 2026, with a margin of error of 4 percent. The poll shows that 48 percent of Hispanics support Donalds and 43 percent would back Jolly. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. news.text:
Psyche! It's a trick question. The correct answer is "every Democrat running for office this cycle."

The Washington Free Beacon's intrepid investigative reporter Chuck Ross dug up these gems from 2021 and 2022, where El-Sayed demands socialized medicine that will fund healthcare for illegal aliens who want sex-change operations, apparently quite the niche for young progressives these days.

Hardest hit: CBS News? Dana Bash? Max Tani?

Abdul El-Sayed, in a series of unearthed podcast remarks, called for a "truly inclusive" universal health care entitlement that would include "care for transgender people" and "care for immigrants." He later criticized conservatives for demonizing "the undocumented person who comes to this country and wants to get gender reassignment surgery on Medicare for All."Transgender immigrants seeking government-funded gender treatments, he said, were the "prime example" that conservatives would use to turn the public against universal health care, "because it captures a group of multiple marginalized people whom they want to cast as being undeserving."El-Sayed made the remarks in 2021 and 2022 in podcasts unearthed by the Washington Free Beacon. El-Sayed—who at the time was a former Michigan gubernatorial candidate working as a commentator and podcaster—called for a "truly inclusive" taxpayer-funded universal health care system that provides the "full gamut of health care that any and everyone would need." Such a plan, he said, should include health care for illegal aliens, transgender people, and transgender illegal aliens seeking sex-change procedures.

I can just see the ads now: Abdul El-Sayed is for they/them/MS-13. Mike Rogers is for you. "That’s going to be the example that they’re going to push forward because it captures a group of multiple marginalized people whom they want to cast as being undeserving," El-Sayed said.

Well, let's talk about "deserving" in this context. El-Sayed and his allies then want to force taxpayers to fund elective surgeries for people who haven't legitimately paid into that closed system at the expense of those who do. 

The comment about the ads is not just a comic aside, either. Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris on this issue with a single ad about funding felons' sex-change operations, even without mentioning socialized medicine or coverage for illegal aliens. Trump won Michigan with that message, at least to a significant extent. Rogers has been aggressive and fast in his messaging, so we can probably expect ads highlighting these issues in the final fortnight. The challenge might be fitting all of these issues into a 30-second spot, so hopefully they have a large inventory of 60-second spots on the home stretch.

news.title: The GOP counts on farmers' votes. As a costly harvest season raises concerns, Trump heads to Kansas
news.text: Fifth-generation Kansas farmer Glenn Brunkow describes this time of year as “go time,” when farmers are combining fields, hauling crops to town and moving livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.But this harvest season, they’re doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits.“It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions,” said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.The economic strain is becoming a growing political concern for Republicans in states they have long dominated. President Donald Trump is heading to Kansas on Monday and Iowa later in the week, the latest in a series of stops where he's trying to energize his base in the final weeks before the midterm elections.The visits come as Republicans pour money into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa amid concerns about voter enthusiasm. The anxiety may be especially notable in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 — as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas in 94 years.Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, has attracted Republican support in his Senate bid, including endorsements from two former GOP governors. In a video statement ahead of Trump’s visit, Hamilton said it was “an honor” to welcome a sitting president to Kansas."I want Kansans to know that if you voted for the president, you also have a place in my campaign,” he added.Brunkow, whose organization endorsed Marshall, said he’s been asked many times whether the economic frustrations could drive Republican farmers to vote for Democrats.“I don’t think it necessarily does that,” Brunkow said. “But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls.”RELATED NEWS | First on Scripps News: Trump is headed back to Texas to campaign for Ken PaxtonRepublican voters' frustrations with the party have deepenedDon Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn't seen Marshall do. She's never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. "I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.“And then of course the trade agreements," she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”RELATED STORY | High inflation and the Iran war put pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm electionsFarmers face a financial squeezeFarmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.The Trump administration has attempted to ease some of those burdens. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump, although he thinks most would still consider him the better choice in the 2024 election.“He’s made some unforced errors," said Brunkow. “Miscalculations, bad advice, that had unintended consequences.”Concerns spread beyond KansasTrump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”A third-generation farmer, Tester said he first began farming in 1978 and witnessed the farm crisis of the 1980s, when “a fair number of my neighbors left town.”“We’re setting up for the same kind of situation,” said Tester. “The economics in family farm production agriculture right now are probably worse right now than they were in the 1980s.”
news.summary: Republicans are pouring money into farm-country Senate races, where the steepening cost of living is top of mind for voters.

news.title: Pollster Frank Luntz CRUSHES Democrats' hopes over favorable polling
news.text:
Polling expert and political strategist Frank Luntz explains why the polls showing a comfortable lead for Democrats are not dependable.

Luntz explained during an appearance on CNN Thursday why many may now be making the same polling mistake he made in 2016 and claimed polling just isn't capturing an accurate picture of the electorate.

'I'm still skeptical. In the end, Republicans are less likely persons to believe the polls.'

"What do you think the polls may be missing? Do you think they're under-sampling the kind of voter that Trump usually brings out, that sort of non-engaged voter that may not respond to a phone call from a pollster?" asked anchor Boris Sanchez.

"We know that they don't respond to phone calls. We know that in the exit polling back in 2016, and I say this publicly because I want people to hear this," Luntz said.

"You know, I teach at West Point. I cannot lie, cheat, or steal. The cadets can't. I can't. I got 2016 wrong. I believed in the exit polls. Trump voters walked away, refused to participate, because they thought that it was against them," he added.

"They thought that the polls were all biased," Luntz said. "And that's what Republicans are being told right now: 'Don't believe the polls. They're not accurate.' Well they may be, we're about to find out."

He went on to say that turnout is the key to the election, and the polling may not be accurately reflecting which group of people actually shows up at the ballot box. 

"I'm still skeptical. In the end, Republicans are less likely to participate. They're less likely to believe the polls are happening. I'm most interested in turnout," he continued. 

"They're polling how the electorate overall feels and not polling the people [that] are actually going to participate. But in the end, who the hell cares?"

RELATED: Pollster Frank Luntz says CNN town hall exposed why Kamala Harris was losing to Trump

Despite the warning about the polling, Luntz also said the president's historically low approval rating would affect Republicans' chances to win the midterm elections.

"That's not good at all, and he's as recently as three weeks ago called affordability a hoax. It's not a hoax if you can't afford eggs. It's not a hoax if you can't afford steak," said Luntz.

"I don't know if they understand how people actually feel, that they are anxious, nervous, angry because their lives are tougher today than they used to be," he added.

He warned that if the polls were indeed correct, Democrats would have a big night on November 3.

news.title: Elon Musk Makes Wild Promise to Every Kid in America
news.text:
Elon Musk, whose personal net worth hovers around $1 trillion, says he plans to give every child in America one share of SpaceX next year.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,“ Musk posted to X, which he owns, on Monday.

SpaceX shares closed Friday at $146.03, ahead of the company’s quarterly earnings report on Tuesday.

At that price, the proposed giveaway would total a whopping $10.5 billion if it covered all 72 million American children under 18. Musk has not specified if there would be any qualifications or explained how he would distribute the shares.

The White House is also pushing for American children to grow wealth with the newly created Trump accounts, which automatically give kids a one-time $1,000 payment from the government.

Musk’s promise follows AI giant Anthropic announcing that it would commit 5 percent of its shares to a public benefit fund. 

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO responded to the post, “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public.”

His announcement also comes as skepticism of AI mounts, becoming a political liability for Republican and Democrat candidates alike.

A Wall Street Journal poll from September found that most Americans support pausing AI development.

Musk has a long history of encouraging people to have kids. He leads by example, with at least 14 children of his own with four different women. 

The tech mogul has repeatedly sounded the alarm bell on slowing population growth, urging people to have more kids. 

He has said that falling birth rates pose a greater risk to society than climate change.

The former face of DOGE has publicly and privately solicited women to bear his children.

While Musk’s former girlfriend Ashley St. Clair was pregnant with his 13th child in 2024, The Wall Street Journal uncovered text messages in which Musk suggested they use surrogates to have more children faster. 

“To reach legion-level before the apocalypse,” he wrote to St. Clair, referring to the thousands of soldiers who made up the armies of ancient Rome.

In a bizarre post, Musk also once offered to give Taylor Swift a child after she endorsed Kamala Harris for president.

news.title: The workplace intelligence double standard: Why clever women are branded 'hostile' - while smart men are treated better
news.text:
Sometimes it’s hard to be a woman, the song goes – and never more so perhaps than when you’re good at your job.

For many successful women, earning colleagues’ respect can feel an impossible task – because they are often seen as cold and hostile, a study has found.

And the price for being clever and female does not stop there, as intelligent men appear to avoid this issue - even reporting better treatment from their peers if they prove highly competent.

The findings may help explain why accomplished women, ranging from Margaret Thatcher and Angela Merkel to Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, have often been called unlikeable despite being widely regarded as highly capable leaders.

'We tend to think of intelligence as an inherently positive attribute in the workplace,' first author Dr Nitya Chawla, from University College London, told the Daily Mail.

'However, our research suggests that intelligence can have very different interpersonal consequences for women and men.'

For their study, the researchers analysed data from more than 800 people across 140 teams.

Participants completed cognitive ability tests and rated colleagues on factors including hostility, support and workplace treatment.

Analysis revealed that very smart women were more likely to be viewed as hostile, receive less help from teammates and report greater workplace mistreatment.

But the findings, published in the Journal of Applied Psychology, also point to a workplace double standard.

Men with similarly high cognitive ability did not experience the same penalties and, in some cases, received more support from colleagues.

The researchers said women who are competent may face a backlash because they are seen to be violating traditional expectations.

'Our findings point to the role of gender stereotypes in shaping how intelligence is interpreted,' Dr Chawla said.

'When women possess intelligence, they automatically are also perceived as less warm and more hostile. 

'Men, however, do not carry the same perceptual burdens.'

The results may help explain why talented women can struggle to gain the same support and recognition as equally competent male colleagues.

The researchers also warned that the consequences can extend far beyond hurt feelings.

They said seemingly minor acts, such as excluding women from informal discussions or withholding support, can build up over time and ultimately damage career prospects.

'These interpersonal experiences are often not limited to a single interaction - rather, they tend to occur repeatedly, shaping women's sense of belonging, access to resources, and ability to thrive at work,' Dr Chawla added.
news.summary: It pays to be clever at work - unless you're female, according to a new study.

news.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
news.text:
A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate. But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris. It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions, primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.

Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.

While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts.

Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.

Benefits of federal investment

Elected officials are sometimes accused of “pork barrel politics,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.

Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.” 

That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.

The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election

Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election. 

During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “economic development opportunities,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself.

Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.

In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.

We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022. 

When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.

Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.

These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.

While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.

Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks

Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases. 

The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands.

This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.

These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.
news.summary: Incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

news.title: Latino Voters Keep Leaning Toward Democrats Ahead of The Midterms as Trump's Approval Falls
news.text: Latino voters are approaching the 2026 midterm elections with greater interest than four years ago, a preference for Democratic congressional candidates and growing dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump, including among some who helped return him to office, new data shows.A new Pew Research Center survey found that more than half of Latino registered voters (51%) support the Democratic House candidate in their district, compared with 24% who favor the Republican. Another 18% remain unsure, while 7% prefer another candidate.Pew surveyed 5,062 adults, including 774 Hispanic registered voters, from September 28 through October 4. The research was conducted in English and Spanish. Among Latino voters backing Democratic House candidates, 77% say control of Congress really matters, up from 58% ahead of the 2022 midterms. The share describing themselves as extremely motivated to vote rose from 41% to 53%.Forty-five percent of Latino Democratic candidate supporters say they have given the upcoming elections considerable thought, compared with 24% four years ago. Latino voters supporting Republican candidates report lower engagement than their Democratic counterparts.Latino registered voters now show interest comparable to other registered voters, closing an engagement gap Pew recorded in 2022. Fifty-five percent of Latino registered voters describe their congressional vote as opposition to the president. Just 14% consider it a vote supporting him, while 30% say he is not much of a factor.That differs substantially from the previous midterms. In 2022, nearly half of Latino voters said President Joe Biden was not a factor in their congressional choice. Trump's approval among Latino registered voters now stands at 24%, down from 38% in February 2025. The decline is steeper within his own 2024 Latino electorate, with 57% approving of his performance, compared with 93% at the beginning of his second term.Among Latinos who voted for Trump in 2024, 65% still favor the Republican House candidate. Eleven percent support the Democrat, while the remaining 24% prefer another candidate or remain undecided. By comparison, 84% of Latino voters who backed Kamala Harris support their Democratic congressional candidate.The economy is Latino voters' leading issue, accompanied by increasingly negative assessments of national conditions and greater concern about gasoline costs and unemployment.Even Latino voters who supported Trump have become more pessimistic. Only 34% rate economic conditions as excellent or good, down from 57% at the start of the year. Their assessments extend beyond household finances.Seventy percent of Latino registered voters say administration policies have harmed Hispanics, while 12% say they have helped. Sixty-one percent say Hispanics' situation in the United States has worsened over the past year.The results follow elections in which Republicans narrowed Democrats' longstanding Latino advantage. Democrats won Latino voters by 47 percentage points in the 2018 midterms, but that margin fell to 21 points in 2022. Trump subsequently won nearly half of Latino votes in 2024.Among registered Latino voters who skipped the 2024 election, Democrats lead Republicans 47% to 18%. But 31% remain unsure whom they would support, leaving a substantial group of potential voters whose preferences are still unsettled.
news.summary: A new survey found that 51% of Latino registered voters support the Democratic House candidate in their district, compared with 24% who favor the Republican.
news.author: Matias Civita

news.title: Talarico and Paxton Face Off With Dueling Rallies in Pivotal Texas County
news.text: Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are taking their Senate fight to Tarrant County on Monday, holding dueling rallies in Fort Worth as Texans cast the first ballots in one of the most competitive Senate races in the country. Tarrant County has swung back-and-forth over the past decade. Former Representative Beto O'Rourke carried it in his 2018 Senate race with 313,497 votes to 309,189 for Senator Ted Cruz, the last time a Democrat below the top of the ticket won the county. In presidential elections, former President Joe Biden edged President Donald Trump there in 2020 by less than a quarter of a percentage point, and Trump took it back in 2024, beating former Vice President Kamala Harris 51.9 percent to 46.7 percent. Both campaigns now see the county as pivotal. Where Are Talarico and Paxton Rallying Today? Talarico and Paxton are holding competing rallies in Fort Worth on Monday as they crisscross the Lone Star State ahead of Election Day. Talarico, an Austin state representative, starts the day with a 1 p.m. rally at the University of North Texas in Denton before heading to North Crowley High School in southwest Fort Worth. Doors open at 6 p.m., with the program scheduled for 7 p.m. His “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour began with a stop in Plano on Sunday. It will continue through East Texas, Houston, the Gulf Coast, San Antonio, South Texas, El Paso and Lubbock before returning to Dallas on October 29. Talarico plans to hold his final rally in Austin on November 2. Paxton, the state's attorney general, will also rally in Fort Worth at 7 p.m., joined by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. His campaign has not publicly announced the venue. The Republican will begin the day in Allen, in Collin County, after stops in Rockwall and Killeen on Saturday and San Antonio on Sunday. GOP Governor Greg Abbott is also scheduled to appear in Fort Worth on Monday. The candidates have offered contrasting messages on the trail. Paxton's “Come and Take It” tour frames him as a defender of Texas values, including Christianity and the oil and gas industry. At a Saturday rally in Rockwall, he accused Talarico of threatening those values and urged supporters to vote early. Talarico has focused on political divisions and Paxton's legal and ethical controversies. At a CNN town hall last Wednesday, he said, “We cannot afford Ken Paxton's corruption.” Talarico Has a Broad Donor Edge in Tarrant County as Paxton Allies Write Big Checks Talarico has built a far wider fundraising base than Paxton in Tarrant County, according to a Newsweek analysis of third-quarter filings covering July 1 to September 30. ZIP codes were assigned to the county where most of their area falls, so county totals are approximate. Talarico's campaign committee took in $730,047 in itemized individual contributions from about 2,560 Tarrant County donors. Paxton's campaign raised $304,148 from about 570. The Democrat outraised the Republican in 66 of the county's 74 ZIP codes and had more donors in 69. Paxton's leads, on the other hand, were small and scattered. The biggest came in Fort Worth's 76114 ZIP code, where six Paxton donors gave $10,059, compared with $3,839 from 21 Talarico donors. Paxton also led narrowly in Euless 76040. Even the Republican-leaning suburbs inside Tarrant broke Talarico's way. Colleyville sent his campaign about $52,700 from 145 donors; Paxton got $27,600 from 45. In Keller, 154 donors gave Talarico $37,700, more than double Paxton's $17,100 from 46. Republican-leaning Suburbs Inside Tarrant CityTalaricoPaxtonColleyville$52,700 from 145 donors$27,600 from 45Southlake$33,400 from 111$26,300 from 42Keller$37,700 from 154$17,100 from 46Grapevine$30,200 from 131$19,500 from 26Mansfield$21,900 from 75$4,100 from 12 Grapevine ran $30,200 from 131 donors for Talarico and $19,500 from 26 for Paxton. Mansfield was lopsided, at $21,900 from 75 donors against $4,100 from 12. Southlake was the closest on money, $33,400 for Talarico to $26,300 for Paxton, though Talarico had nearly three times as many donors there, 111 to 42. In Arlington, the county's largest city after Fort Worth, Talarico raised $121,000 from 427 donors and Paxton $30,700 from 75. Paxton's joint fundraising committee scrambles that math. Paxton Victory collected about $703,000 from just seven Tarrant County donors, most of them in west Fort Worth. Seven checkbooks, in other words, roughly matched what some 2,560 people in the county gave Talarico's campaign. The two largest checks came from Seth Crawford, who gave $274,300, of which the committee later refunded $8,500, and Gary Blake, who gave $200,000. Paxton Victory also funds the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSS) and a leadership PAC, so not all of that money goes to Paxton's campaign. Talarico has far more people giving in Tarrant. Paxton has a handful of wealthy allies writing checks big enough to close much of the distance. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: What Latest Polls Show The newest survey landed on the eve of early voting. A University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs poll of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 10 to 14 and released Sunday night, found Talarico ahead 48 percent to 46 percent, with a margin of error of 2.19 percentage points. Libertarian Ted Brown drew 3 percent, and 3 percent were unsure. Republican defections account for a good part of the margin. In that poll, 98 percent of likely Democratic voters backed Talarico, while 88 percent of likely Republican voters backed Paxton, and 6 percent of Republicans said they would vote for the Democrat. Independents favored Talarico 60 percent to 32 percent. Mark Jones, a political science fellow at Rice University's Baker Institute who worked on the survey, told Newsweek that O'Rourke trailed Cruz in nearly every poll at this point in 2018, while Talarico leads in most surveys now, sometimes by only a point or two. The suburbs are where Jones sees the difference. Paxton is “deadlocked with Talarico in the suburban areas,” he said, a problem for a party that relies on “running up the numbers in the suburban areas to make up for the losses that they always experience in the big urban areas like Houston, Dallas, Austin and San Antonio.” Most other October surveys look similar. A CBS News/YouGov poll of 1,458 likely voters, taken October 8 to 16, had Talarico up 51 percent to 49 percent. The University of Texas/Texas Politics Project, which fields its surveys through YouGov, found him ahead 50 percent to 47 percent among 861 likely voters questioned September 25 to October 5. Marist's poll of 1,196 likely voters, conducted October 8 to 11, put Talarico at 47 percent and Paxton at 45 percent, with 6 percent unsure, though a majority of respondents expected Paxton to win anyway. ActiVote, working with a much smaller sample of 400 likely voters, gave Talarico a 4-point edge, 52 percent to 48 percent. Paxton led in only one of the six most recent public surveys. InsiderAdvantage had him ahead 49 percent to 48 percent among 1,200 likely voters polled October 13 and 14. "He was losing, and he's leading," Trump said last week of Paxton, giving the rallies credit for the turn. When Does Early Voting Begin in Texas? Early voting began Monday, October 19, and runs through Friday, October 30. Texans can vote at any early voting site in their county of registration, and Election Day is November 3. Voters must show an acceptable photo ID, such as a Texas driver's license or a Texas Election Identification Certificate. The pool of voters is the largest in state history. Secretary of State Robert Howden announced last week that Texas has 19,041,684 registered voters, up 2.2 percent from the November 2024 general election. Why the Texas Senate Race Matters in 2026 Midterm Elections Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, making the seat one of the few places where Democrats can play offense as they try to overturn the Republicans' 53-47 majority. Paxton reached November after a bruising primary. Senator John Cornyn sought reelection but lost the nomination to Paxton in a May runoff, and Trump endorsed Paxton on May 19. During the primary, Cornyn and Senate Majority Leader John Thune warned that a Democrat could beat Paxton if he became the nominee. The race has become the most expensive contest of the 2026 midterm cycle, and Talarico's latest quarterly haul tripled Paxton's. The broader ballot is less favorable to Democrats. In the gubernatorial race, Abbott leads Austin Democrat Gina Hinojosa by 3 points, and other statewide Republicans lead by 5 to 7 points. Tarrant County, where Abbott and Paxton campaign on Monday, will test how much ticket-splitting Talarico can count on. Forecasters see it as a coin flip. The Cook Political Report moved Texas from "Lean Republican" to "Toss Up" in August, and the race has stayed there. In its most recent Senate overview, published October 6, Cook shifted Kansas to "Toss Up" too and wrote that a Senate majority is now squarely within Democrats' reach. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editor for this story: Anthony Murray and Jason Lemon.
news.summary: Talarico and Paxton hold dueling Fort Worth rallies as early voting opens in Tarrant County, the swing county both camps covet.

news.title: Trump's Kansas Approval Rating Ahead of Rally as GOP Senate Seat at Risk
news.text: President Donald Trump is heading to Kansas for a campaign event on Monday as polls show a tightening Senate race between Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton in a seat Republicans have held for nearly a century. Trump is scheduled to campaign near Wichita just weeks before the November 3 election, as Democrats are increasingly optimistic about taking control of the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. The Kansas Senate race has emerged as among the tossups that could determine which party holds a majority when Congress reconvenes next year. The president has traversed the country in recent weeks to try to boost candidates who are supportive of his policies, including several candidates running in competitive races in traditionally conservative states. The national environment has shifted in Democrats’ favor as Trump’s approval rating has slipped in recent months amid growing voter frustration with the economy, largely centered around affordability and the cost of living. Kansas, a farm state, could also be particularly vulnerable to impacts of soaring diesel prices amid the Iran war. Republicans will be hoping the Trump rally could build enthusiasm among the conservative base to head to the polls in November, but Democrats are still optimistic after a flurry of surveys have shown the race could be decided by a razor-thin margin. Kansas has long been a conservative stronghold, the Democrats last winning a Senate race there in 1932. In a statement to Newsweek, the Marshall campaign described the election as a "clear choice" between a senator who has "delivered major wins for our farmers, cut taxes for the middle class, and secured the border" or a "Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat." "We look forward to welcoming President Trump to Kansas today—a president who is second to none at getting out the vote," the statement reads. Newsweek reached out to the Hamilton campaign for comment via email. Donald Trump’s Approval Rating in Kansas Three recent polls reveal that Trump’s approval rating is underwater in Kansas, despite him winning the state by 16 points against former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. Trump’s net approval rating was -7 points in a recent YouGov poll of 2,255 likely voters conducted from September 24 to October 4. Forty-six percent of respondents said they approved of Trump, while 53 percent disapproved of him, the poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points, found. Meanwhile, a The New York Times/ Siena poll gave him a -15 point approval rating, with 40 percent approving and 55 percent disapproving. It surveyed 605 voters from September 22 to 30, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.6 percentage points. In an Emerson College poll, 53 percent of respondents disapproved of Trump while 40 percent approved, giving him a -13 point approval rating among 750 likely voters. The poll was conducted from September 15 to 16 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Roger Marshall vs. Adam Hamilton: What Kansas Senate Race Polls Show Although Kansas is not traditionally seen as competitive in federal races, polling has shown a tight race between Hamilton and Marshall. The YouGov poll gave Hamilton a 3-point lead over Marshall, 48 percent to 45 percent, while the Times poll showed a dead heat, with each candidate receiving support from 45 percent of respondents. Meanwhile, the Emerson poll showed Hamilton up 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent. A recent poll from InsiderAdvantage, however, showed Marshall up a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. It was conducted among 1,200 likely voters from October 13 to 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Democrats view Hamilton, who is a well-known pastor in the state, as a strong candidate against Marshall, who was first elected in 2020. But Republicans are hopeful the partisan lean of the Sunflower State will keep the seat in GOP hands this November. An Emerging Battleground? Democrats have eyed Kansas in recent cycles as a potential future battleground, as the state has trended leftward over the past few decades. In 2024, Trump carried Kansas by about 16 points. He won it by about 15 points in 2020 and 20 points in 2016. Mitt Romney won Kansas by nearly 22 points in 2012, while John McCain won it by about 15 points in 2008. Former President George W. Bush won Kansas by 25 points in 2004 and 21 points in 2000. Kansas City suburbs have fueled Democrats’ hope that the state could become less rigidly conservative. Areas around Johnson County have rapidly become more Democratic, but the state overall still favors Republicans. The state is led by Democratic Governor Laura Kelly, who won in 2018 and 2022. Democrats also made a play for Kansas’ Senate race in 2020, but Marshall defeated Democrat Barbara Bollier by more than 11 points. This year, Kansas is also facing impacts of rising diesel fuel, as the state has a large agricultural economic sector. Diesel is important to farmers for several reasons. Heavy agricultural machinery, including tractors, harvesters, and irrigation pumps, use diesel engines. Rising diesel prices translate to higher operating costs for farmers. It also powers trucks, trains and ships that move agricultural products across the supply chain, increasing transportation costs across the industry. Diesel prices averaged $6.0722 in Kansas on Monday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). That is lower than the $6.2039 average one month earlier, but still higher than the average of $3.3907 one year ago. Hamilton has also held stronger fundraising than Marshall. In the third quarter of 2026, the Democratic candidate raised nearly $10 million, while Marshall raised less than $1 million. What Prediction Markets Show Marshall remains the favorite to win reelection on prediction markets. He had a 61 percent chance on Kalshi and a 63 percent chance on Polymarket of defeating Hamilton. Still, that is narrower than one month earlier, when his chances stood at around 74 percent in both markets. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. What Happens Next Hamilton and Marshall will spend the next two weeks making their final pitches to voters across Kansas in hopes of motivating their bases, while also winning over any remaining undecided voters. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classify the race as a pure toss-up. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Trevor Davies
news.summary: Polls point to a close race for a seat Democrats have not won in nearly a century in this year's midterms.

news.title: Trump creates new women’s health division at NIH and taps Susie Wiles to lead task force
news.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday to create a new women's health division at the National Institutes of Health and a dedicated White House task force to bolster federal research into women's health.

The initiative was pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump, and the panel was set to hold its first meeting after a Rose Garden ceremony attended by the Trumps.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed breast cancer treatment, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the task force, which will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs, the Trump administration said. No specific funding goals were included in the order.

“Beginning today we will change the reality of women’s health,” Melania Trump said at the Monday event. “Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”

The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women.”

Beyond research, the order is intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment. It calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. Other health concerns and diseases are also mentioned, including Alzheimer's, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke.

The first lady helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady and it followed a series of meetings she had with federal health officials.

The president called it a "historic action” and praised the first lady's work.

“She’s accomplished so much,” he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn.

Returning to women's health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order's requirements had not already been imposed.

“Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?” he said, after recalling that he'd asked Melania Trump, “Are you sure they don't have that?”

In Trump's second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. During Trump's first presidency, her signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse.

The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as the president's job approval ratings have declined, including among women.

About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls.

That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump's hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war.
news.summary: The president called the initiative a ‘historic action’ and praised First Lady Melania Trump’s work on it

news.title: Police Officer Fired for Sharing Her Flock Safety Login With ICE Agent Husband
news.text: A Savannah Georgia police officer Amber Harpe gave her husband, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, access to the police department’s Flock license plate reader system, which he used to conduct hundreds of searches tied to ICE investigations across the Southeast. The Savannah Police Officer has now been fired for handing her Flock System Credentials to her ICE agent husband Critics claim the case underscores severe vulnerabilities in how law enforcement agencies monitor automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks and secure sensitive tracking infrastructure. Savannah Police Officer Amber Harpe admitted to giving her department username and password directly to her husband an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent who confirmed he requested the credentials because he lacked direct access to the Flock system through DHS. The internal investigation was triggered after an audit flagged an abnormal surge of searches running through Harpe’s account between January and July 2026. In total, the audit uncovered 983 search entries tracking 97 identifiable plates across six states: Georgia, New Jersey, Maryland, Florida, North Carolina, and South Carolina. South Carolina plates dominated the activity, accounting for 788 search entries across 48 plates. Furthermore, internal documents noted that the majority of the registered vehicle owners flagged during the audit were Hispanic. While Harpe's husband maintained that every query targeted individuals with active federal arrest warrants and claimed he stopped using the account once ICE shifted operations, the Savannah Police Department took a zero tolerance stance. Because her husband was an ICE agent using the queries for federal immigration enforcement and warrant lookups (rather than financial or commercial gain), the case currently sits primarily in the realm of internal employment discipline and agency policy violations rather than an active criminal prosecution. Tyler Harpe estimated that he used the account for about four months. He said he stopped roughly three weeks before his interview because the agency no longer conducted vehicle stops and he no longer needed the system. Harpe gave investigators a slightly different timeline, saying her husband stopped about a week before her interview because he was concerned she could face discipline. He denied searching for relatives, former romantic partners or anyone for personal reasons. He maintained that every person he searched was an ICE target and said the Flock information helped his agency locate wanted people with criminal histories. He also acknowledged that using another officer’s account could violate policy. “The investigation established that Amber Harpe provided her Flock Safety credentials to her husband,” the final report said. “Both provided consistent statements that the searches involved ICE targets and were conducted for law-enforcement purposes.” Savannah is considered a liberal and Democratic-leaning city, though it exists inside a solid conservative region. In Chatham County both Joe Biden and Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump by a wide margin.

news.title: There's a chance JD Vance may not run for president in 2028
news.text:
JD Vance's commitment to his family may come ahead of his presidential run.

The vice president, during CBS News' town hall on Oct. 18, said “there’s a chance” he won’t run for president in 2028.

“Of course there’s a chance,” Vance, a frontrunner to succeed Donald Trump as Republican nominee, said when asked by host "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil if there's any chance he won't run.

"Man, we've got four little kids," Vance said, adding his wife, second lady Usha Vance "has never loved politics."

"She loves public service,” Vance said. “I think you know you can do a lot of good in this job, and I’ve tried to do as much good as possible.”

More news: JD Vance says he's focused on doing 'God's work,' speaks on 'end times'

JD, Usha Vance recently welcomed baby boy

The Vances are parents to four children. The couple welcomed their youngest child, Alec Neel Vance, on July 19 at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland.

"We are excited to announce that our baby boy, Alec Neel Vance, was born this morning," the Vance family said in a statement on social media at the time. "Usha and the baby are happy and healthy, and our kids are overjoyed to meet their little brother."

Alec joins his siblings Ewan, 9, Vivek, 6, and Mirabel, 4. 

VP says he's a 'procrastinator'

Vance said most people assume that he's going to run for president, but that he actually hates thinking about it.

"The way that I think about life, big life decisions – my wife will tell you this – is I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," Vance said.

However, he hinted he plans to give the question more serious consideration after the November midterm elections.

"Anything could happen, man," Vance said before redirecting the conversation once again to the upcoming midterms, saying the goal is to "elect as many good candidates as possible."

Polls show Vance is a frontrunner for 2028

Vance's comments come as the buzz around potential 2028 presidential candidates grows, and a new poll shows him as the clear frontrunner in a hypothetical GOP primary.

A new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released Sunday, Oct. 11, revealed Vance and former Vice President Kamala Harris both led their respective party’s potential primary.

According to the survey, Vance leads with 38% of Republicans, followed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 24%, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis receiving 9% of support from GOP respondents.

Usha Vance keeping 'open mind' on JD Vance's potential presidential run

Usha Vance, in an interview with Fox News' "Fox & Friends" that aired Aug. 26, said she was open to whatever her husband chose to do ahead of 2028 and was taking it “one step at a time” as the vice president focuses on the midterm general election on Nov. 3.

"Whatever it is that he feels is the right thing for him to do, we're going to have a good time doing it," she told host Rachel Campos-Duffy. “We will make the best of it in the best possible way."

Contributing: Fernando Cervantes Jr., USA TODAY

news.title: Trump takes border crackdown to deep-red state as shock Senate battle threatens GOP stronghold
news.text: EXCLUSIVE: WICHITA, KANSAS — President Donald Trump is expected to tout his immigration agenda in ruby-red Kansas on Monday, weeks after federal immigration agents made dozens of arrests in the southwestern portion of the state. Trump is headed to the Sunflower State for a rally just outside of Wichita as a tighter-than-expected Senate race that could determine the balance of power in the upper chamber unfolds. Fox News Digital has learned that Trump will lean into the policy positions that helped propel him and Republicans to power two years ago. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER "President Trump stopped the invasion of our country and delivered Americans the most secure border in American history," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Under the President’s leadership, 3 million illegals have left the United States and zero illegals have been released at the border in seventeen months." "Meanwhile, radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies, abolish ICE, and grant amnesty to the illegal aliens they released into our communities," she continued. The Trump-led Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have touted a string of arrests and deportations of illegal immigrants in the state over the last several months. GEORGIA ICE SWEEP NABS OVER 700 CRIMINAL ILLEGAL ALIENS, INCLUDING SEX OFFENDERS, CHILD ABUSERS According to the White House, among some of the "worst of the worst" who were arrested in the state by federal immigration officers include Omar Israel Hernandez of Mexico, convicted of first-degree murder, Jose Luis Rauda-Diaz of El Salvador, convicted of aggravated robbery and two counts of possession of a weapon, Oscar Sanchez-Corona of Mexico, who had previously been deported for drug offenses, damaging property, and driving under the influence, Greg Chukwuka Orji of Nigeria, convicted of dangerous drugs and possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, and Alberto Estrada of Mexico, convicted of aggravated indecent liberties with a child and rape. Trump’s rally comes as the race between Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton has cranked up in a state the president has won by double-digits in the last three presidential cycles and has given Republicans cause for concern in a state where voters haven’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan race ranker, downgraded the contest to a toss-up earlier this month and money from GOP and Democratic groups is flowing into the state. KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ Marshall, who is vying for a second term, has run close to Trump, rarely breaking from him on key issues throughout this cycle. Hamilton, however, has run away from the Democratic establishment in Washington, D.C., and warned that if elected, he wouldn’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term leading the caucus. Trump’s appearance in the state also follows ICE’s three-day sweep in Southwest Kansas last month, dubbed "Operation Safe Community — Kansas," where agents made over 100 arrests. Marshall pushed back on the operation, demanding that "when ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement." "Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe," Marshall said on X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, Republicans have targeted Hamilton for his immigration stance, accusing him through ads run by outside groups, like the Senate Leadership Fund, of supporting mass amnesty. Hamilton, however, pushed back on the Biden administration’s immigration policies and told the Johnson County Post that the previous administration's open border policies "caused a different kind of chaos." "Record crossings overwhelmed communities, and the immigration courts fell years behind," Hamilton said. "I’m not for open borders, and dangerous criminals don’t belong here."

news.title: Exclusive: Kamala Harris Is Teaming Up With the NAACP to Get Voters Ready for November
news.text:
Kamala Harris is heading back into the community, and this time, the focus is on making sure voters understand what’s at stake before they head to the polls. The NAACP announced that its president and CEO, Derrick Johnson, will join the former vice president for community conversations in Milwaukee on Oct. 26 and Atlanta on Oct. 29. The events are part of the organization’s broader push to educate, engage and mobilize voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

For the nation’s oldest and largest civil rights organization, this is about more than a couple of fireside chats and a few photo ops. It’s about connecting the issues affecting Black communities to the political decisions that shape everyday life.

“The NAACP has been at the forefront of protecting voting rights and ensuring our communities have a voice in our democracy,” Johnson said in a statement to The Root. “Our work doesn’t begin or end on Election Day. From voter education to grassroots organizing, we remain committed to building informed, engaged communities. We look forward to continuing that work alongside Vice President Harris in Milwaukee and Atlanta.”

For Black folks in Milwaukee and Atlanta, that means confronting questions about affordability, economic opportunity, health care access and voting rights — issues that can feel a whole lot more urgent than the political noise coming out of Washington.

RELATED: Expert: The NAACP is Fighting to Keep Black Communities From Becoming AI’s Collateral Damage

The NAACP is a non-partisan organization. Still, the latest collaboration with the former Democratic vice president comes at a critical time for Black Americans across the country, especially in the South. 

In metro Atlanta, housing affordability topped the list of regional concerns in the Atlanta Regional Commission’s 2025 Metro Atlanta Speaks survey. Twenty-eight percent of respondents identified housing costs as the region’s biggest problem, followed by traffic at 24%. More than six in 10 said they couldn’t afford to move to another home or apartment in their current neighborhood. Those numbers reflect the wider region, not Black residents alone, but they underscore the economic pressures facing communities across metro Atlanta. 

That’s exactly where civic engagement enters the conversation: Who gets elected can influence decisions on housing, jobs, public services and access to health care. Voting alone won’t solve those problems, but disengagement can leave communities with fewer opportunities to hold decision-makers accountable.

Harris laid out the stakes in a fundraising email this month. “For the past twenty months, the American people have struggled as a consequence of the cruelty and corruption of this current administration,” she wrote, according to the Associated Press. “Now is the time for us to be ruthless in delivering for the people: on affordability, on fighting corruption, and on making our voices heard.”

The NAACP is putting serious organizing muscle behind that message. Its multi-million-dollar Get Out the Vote campaign aims to mobilize more than 6.5 million voters across 14 states and 33 congressional districts. The organization says it has recruited more than 52,000 volunteers, who are helping with canvassing, phone banking, door-knocking and digital outreach. 

The organization is also partnering with civil rights and community groups on National Black Man Voter Day, scheduled for Oct. 24, to mobilize 100,000 Black men ahead of early voting.
news.summary:
Kamala Harris is joining Derrick Johnson for a pair of community conversations as the NAACP ramps up its nationwide voter mobilization efforts ahead of November.
