news.title: Troy Jackson Has No Regrets Telling Susan Collins To ‘Shut Up’
news.text: Maine Democratic Senate hopeful Troy Jackson says he has no regrets about telling his rival, incumbent Republican Susan Collins, to "shut up" while the candidates squared off during the final preelection debate. Jackson and Collins sparred last week over President Donald Trump, campaign finances and immigration enforcement in an intense encounter. The debate was briefly interrupted by a data center protester as Collins was speaking. “This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins responded. Jackson fired back, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” The remark toward the sitting senator drew criticism, including from Collins. Jackson refused to apologize during a CNN appearance on Sunday. “She said that it was a Troy supporter," Jackson said of Collins during the interview on State of the Union. "I mean...She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was. I was surprised when he jumped up out of there.” Newsweek has contacted both campaigns for comment. Collins Calls Jackson’s Remark ‘Very Telling’ Last week's debate was the final before Election Day on November 3. The other encounters followed a similar theme, with Collins touting her experience and record of bipartisanship, and Jackson underscoring her political proximity to Trump. Jackson on Sunday said he has tried to be cordial when dealing with the incumbent senator, but that he objected to the implication he had any hand in Thursday night’s interruption. “I’ve had four debates with Senator Collins. I’ve shook her hand afterwards every time. What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins, I’m not going to be accused of things like that. I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me so I’m not going to apologize for that,” he said. Jackson also said groups backing Collins had spent millions "attacking me and my family" with "untrue claims." Collins, in an interview with Fox News following the debate, called the speed of Jackson’s retort “very telling,” and said that it was unsurprising given “the reputation Troy Jackson has and particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees.” Collins had in the past accused Jackson of struggling “to control his temper,” alluding to allegations that the Democrat has been confrontational with colleagues during his time as a state lawmaker. Jackson has denied those allegations. The senator’s campaign told CBS News affiliate WGME that this was “yet another example of Troy Jackson’s angry outbursts with female colleagues, and it raises a serious question about how he handles women who disagree with him.” A Jackson campaign spokeswoman, Maggie Amjad, told the New York Times that the opposing campaign’s attempt “to turn that exchange into anything else is baseless.” Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins: The Latest State of Play The latest Polymarket odds give Jackson a 58 percent chance of winning the crucial Senate seat, and the Democrat has led in the majority of polls since entering the race in late July after Democratic primary winner Graham Platner stepped down amid controversy. A recent poll from InsiderAdvantage shows Jackson with a two-point edge over Collins, similar to one in a survey released Wednesday by Suffolk University. The latter polled 500 Maine voters between October 8 and October 11, with Jackson getting 49 percent support compared to Collins’s 47 percent. Four percent of respondents said they were undecided. Jackson’s leads in most cases have fallen within margins of error, and Collins has in the past demonstrated an ability to overcome significant polling disadvantages. Ahead of the 2020 elections, the final polling averages had Collins trailing Sara Gideon by nearly four points, but the Republican went on to win the race easily, 51 percent to 42 percent. Latest Developments in the Maine Senate Race Between Collins and Jackson With only two weeks to go until November 3, the Maine Senate race is crucial for both party's hopes to carry the majority in the upper chamber. Democrats must defend all their seats and flip four GOP seats to take control. Maine, along with North Carolina, is one of the only targets in a state where Kamala Harris defeated Trump in 2024. Both the Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball rate the race as a toss-up. Both candidates continue to campaign across Maine—touting their records while attacking their opponent on experience, proximity to the Trump administration and campaign financing. Last week, Jackson’s campaign filed its first financial disclosure form with the Federal Election Commission (FEC), which showed that Jackson outraised Collins four-to-one in the most recent quarter, though he remains behind in overall fundraising and outside assistance. Jackson has secured an endorsement from former President Barack Obama and campaigned with progressive firebrand Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren rallied alongside Jackson in Portland, Maine, on Saturday. Speaking on the national “No Kings” day of action, Warren urged Mainers to vote for Jackson as a defense against Trump’s agenda. “You can either have a rubber stamp for a wannabe king, or you can have a fighter for the people,” Warren said. “My money is on Troy Jackson.” And representatives for Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have said that the New York congresswoman will hold a town hall with Jackson in Portland this week. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: Jackson refused to apologize and said groups backing Collins had spent millions "attacking me and my family" with "untrue claims."

news.title: Trump heads to Kansas amid concerns over a costly harvest season
news.text:
For Glenn Brunkow, a fifth-generation farmer in Kansas, autumn is famously "go time," a busy period spent harvesting fields, transporting yields to town, and transferring livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.

This year, agricultural workers are navigating the harvest alongside diesel fuel prices that have climbed by more than $2.50 per gallon compared to last year, compounding pressures from rising costs, volatile markets and shrinking profits.

"It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions," said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.

The economic struggles are becoming a significant political issue for Republicans in states long considered party strongholds. President Donald Trump is traveling to Kansas on Monday before visiting Iowa later in the week, marking his latest effort to energize his base in the final weeks leading up to the midterm elections.

The travel comes as Republicans direct substantial funds into Senate contests in Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa to offset concerns over voter engagement. The concern is particularly acute in Kansas—where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by 16 percentage points in 2024—as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Kansas Senate race in 94 years.

Brunkow, whose group endorsed Marshall, said he is frequently asked whether financial hardship could push Republican farmers to vote Democratic.

"I don’t think it necessarily does that," Brunkow said. "But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls."

Don Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.

He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.

“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”

Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.

“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”

Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn't seen Marshall do. She's never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.

“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. "I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”

Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.

“And then of course the trade agreements," she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”

Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.

Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.

“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.

The Trump administration has attempted to ease some of those burdens. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.

Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump, although he thinks most would still consider him the better choice in the 2024 election.

“He’s made some unforced errors," said Brunkow. “Miscalculations, bad advice, that had unintended consequences.”

Trump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.

In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.

David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.

“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”

Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.

Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.

“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”

A third-generation farmer, Tester said he first began farming in 1978 and witnessed the farm crisis of the 1980s, when “a fair number of my neighbors left town.”

“We’re setting up for the same kind of situation,” said Tester. “The economics in family farm production agriculture right now are probably worse right now than they were in the 1980s.”

news.title: Trump signs an order aimed at boosting women's health research, a plan backed by the first lady
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women's health, a move pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump.

The Republican president signed an executive order that creates a new women’s health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force to focus on the issue. That panel was set to hold its first meeting Monday after the Trumps held a Rose Garden signing ceremony.

“Beginning today we will change the reality of women’s health,” Melania Trump said. “Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”

The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women.” The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment. 

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals. 

The initiative comes after a series of meetings the first lady had with federal health officials. 

The president called it a "historic action” and praised the first lady's work.

“She’s accomplished so much,” he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn.

Shifting back to women's health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order's requirements had not already been imposed. 

“Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?” he said, after recalling that he'd asked Melania Trump, “Are you sure they don't have that?”

The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer’s, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke. 

Melania Trump helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady.

In Donald Trump's second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. In Trump's first presidency, the first lady's signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse.

The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump's job approval ratings have declined, including among women. 

About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls. That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump's hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war.

news.title: STATE OF MONDAY: The People Are Pulling Back — The Billionaires Are Writing Checks
news.text:
Below is State of the Day, a morning newsletter from the Daily Caller Editorial Desk. Sign up here.__________

Hey everyone,

Welcome to State of the Day,

Remember when Trump promised to fight for the little guy?

The People Are Pulling Back — The Billionaires Are Writing Checks

Senate campaigns have tallied their third-quarter cash hauls; the contrast is about as subtle as a brick through a window.

Across nine Senate races, Democrats brought in $231.2 million in the third quarter. Republicans? A meager $48.5 million.

In case you’re just as bad at math as I am, that’s nearly five times as much cash flowing into Democratic campaigns.

James Talarico alone raked in an eye-watering $64 million, with his campaign reporting 97 percent of donations were under $100. When Axios told GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno about Talarico’s haul, Moreno responded, “Oh my God, holy crap. I mean, that’s a number that’s mind-blowing.”

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff wasn’t doing too bad himself, pulling in $33.1 million from more than 760,000 contributions, averaging just $46 apiece.

Turns out, a whole lot of regular folk tossing in a few bucks can build one hell of a war chest. But it’s more than the bank statements. It’s who’s opening their wallets, who’s closing them, and what that means for November.

Trump won in ‘24 by assembling a coalition of working-class, young, and disaffected voters. He promised lower prices, good jobs, and a government that had their backs.

Two years later, that coalition is cracking.

A Wall Street Journal poll found that voters under 30 favor the Democratic candidate by 20 points on a general ballot. In 2024, Trump lost the group to Kamala Harris by four points.

Swing voters, if you will.

Then there’s the economy — the issue that put Trump back into the White House. 

An AP-NORC poll found that just 17 percent of Americans approve his handling of the cost of living. 

The war in Iran? Sixty-nine percent said it hadn’t been worth fighting.

So Americans are still dealing with the cost of living, the administration is embroiled in an expensive war, and Republicans have spent 2 years with a Washington trifecta. 

The party of the working man?

But the GOP has a backup plan. And it’s got a lot of zeros.

According to The Washington Post’s latest breakdown of political megadonors, the 50 biggest donors have poured roughly $2.39 billion into the midterms. Republican-aligned donors account for $1.54 billion of that, compared with $590 million from Democratic-aligned donors.

Elon Musk alone has thrown $369 million into the electoral cycle. I guess, when your fundraising operation starts slacking off, you call the world’s richest man.

To be fair, Democrats have their own wealthy benefactors. George Soros has given $102 million, according to WaPo. 

It’s important to note these are different pools of money — candidate fundraising on one hand and donors financing political groups on the other. 

Trump built his political identity around taking on the elites. Now his party is relying on the fortunes of the ultrawealthy while its working-class coalition has run to the other side of the aisle.

And don’t get me wrong, billionaires can buy a lot of thirty-second ads. But they can’t make groceries cheaper by writing a check to a super PAC. Or convince a trucker that six-dollar diesel is a bargain, let alone why an unjustified war is worth the bill.

And they certainly can’t make voters forget that the party that promised to drain the swamp has become awfully comfortable taking money from the very people it’s supposed to serve, making sure the swamp stays full.

The billionaires aren’t going anywhere anytime soon … the voters? A different story altogether. 

And if the polling, fundraising numbers, and economic frustration are any indication, Republicans have a problem no super PAC can solve.

From The Editors’ Desk

The Iran War Is Going To Go Ballistic After Midterms, Daily Caller News Foundation, Francis Kapper

The Daily Caller News Foundation’s Francis Kapper reveals the Trump administration could soon escalate its unpopular war with Iran, citing senior military officials. While the Trump administration has reduced the frequency of strikes against targets in Iran ahead of the midterm elections, the Pentagon appears prepared for a sharp uptick in military actions after Election Day. 

Here Are the Most Unhinged Ads From The Nearly $80,000,000 AI Slop Spree, Daily Caller News Foundation, Dylan Kresak

The 2026 midterms are the first U.S. election cycle to see widespread use of artificial intelligence (AI) in political advertising, with a whopping $80 million ad spend. The Daily Caller News Foundation’s Dylan Kresak gives a rundown of the good, the bad, and the ugly of 2026’s AI ad splurge — warning: it is mostly ugly. 

Trump Blames France Violence On Immigration, The Telegraph, Vivian Song

U.S. President Donald Trump urged France to close its borders in the face of mounting civil unrest in the country due to a student strike that has been joined by a number of 2nd- and 3rd-generation migrants. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. 

“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social over the weekend. 

Musk Vows to Give Each U.S. Child a SpaceX Share, The Wall Street Journal, Gareth Vipers

The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, pledged to give every child in the U.S. a share of his private space technology company, SpaceX. With millions of children up for the gift, the total could be worth around $10 billion. “This will be the first of many,” Musk said when he announced the plan. news.title: Washington Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez Fights for Trump Country
news.text:
CHEHALIS, Wash. – Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez walked through a county fairgrounds south of Seattle carrying an unremarkable kitchen knife and two pairs of rusted scissors.

She brought the tools to Beverly Phoenix, who was bent over a table in the rear of an exhibit hall, volunteering to restore old household items for local residents. This time, Phoenix was showing a member of Congress how to use a Dremel, a handheld oscillating tool, to sharpen the blades.

The low-key campaign stop underscored Gluesenkamp Perez’s message of self-reliance. She owns an auto repair shop with her husband and has built her political identity around bridging the gaps between urban and rural communities, blue-collar and white-collar workers, and the political left and right.

For Democrats seeking to regain control of the U.S. House, holding districts like this one in Southwest Washington will be essential. Voters there have elected Gluesenkamp Perez twice while also backing President Donald Trump in each of his campaigns. As the party debates how much influence to give its growing progressive movement, making room for moderate and unconventional Democrats could prove just as important to building and preserving a lasting majority.

“We are a really independent community. What we want is respect for our priorities, for our values,” Gluesenkamp Perez said. When her views clash with Democratic leaders, she said, her responsibility is “explaining my community to D.C., not letting D.C. try to define my community’s priorities.”

At 38, Gluesenkamp Perez faces a substantially different challenge this year. Her previous two races were against Republican Joe Kent, who had ties to extremists. Her current opponent, John Braun, is a businessman and state legislator viewed as more mainstream and potentially better positioned to attract moderate voters in the district.

Gluesenkamp Perez is a lightning rod for progressive criticism

The Pacific Northwest is widely seen as a progressive stronghold, but Washington’s 3rd Congressional District defies easy political labels. It includes the northern edge of the Portland, Oregon, metropolitan area as well as broad rural stretches where fishing, logging and manufacturing drive the economy.

Navigating those competing interests has sometimes left Gluesenkamp Perez among the small number of Democrats willing to join Republicans on key votes.

She opposed President Joe Biden’s student debt relief plan and backed a Republican election proposal supported by Trump. She also voted for the Laken Riley immigration bill and defense legislation containing restrictions on abortion and climate initiatives.

Gluesenkamp Perez voted to censure fellow Democratic Reps. Al Green of Texas and Rashida Tlaib. She also introduced a resolution seeking to reprimand Democratic Rep. Chuy Garcia for quietly maneuvering to effectively give his seat to a trusted aide.

The divide surfaced again last month, when Gluesenkamp Perez voted with Republicans twice on procedural matters. Such defections are considered particularly significant on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers are generally expected to follow their party leaders on those votes.

Those votes allowed Republicans to force consideration of a resolution condemning socialism, placing some Democrats in an uncomfortable position during an election year.

“I get upset with her too at times, but you know, I also understand that she represents 800,000-plus people and that’s 800,000-plus opinions for differing views,” said Dale Benjamin, a 66-year-old retiree and self-described “Bernie progressive” from Battle Ground. “I’m very thankful to her that she’s willing to do that, especially in such a divisive place and time that we’re in right now.”

Gluesenkamp Perez has focused much of her legislative work on strengthening her blue-collar credentials and supporting the industries that define her district. She is a prominent advocate for “right to repair” legislation, which would allow consumers and independent businesses to fix tractors, cars and digital devices without relying on the manufacturers.

She has also taken on the sea lions gathering near dams on the Columbia River, where they eat salmon and steelhead before the fish reach fishermen. Gluesenkamp Perez has pushed legislation to make it easier to kill the animals, which she has called “Corolla-sized vermin.”

“People sometimes treat my agenda like it’s like quirky, and I’m like, this is actually very normal where I’m from,” Gluesenkamp Perez said.

More moderate Democrats are likely headed to Washington

Democrats cannot regain control of the House without capturing at least a dozen districts that voted for Trump.

If they succeed, many of the party’s newest lawmakers — the candidates who could deliver a House majority — may look more like Gluesenkamp Perez than the democratic socialists who won a series of primaries in heavily Democratic districts this year.

Democratic leaders will need an agenda that speaks to moderates if they want to stay in power, said Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at Third Way, a Democratic group that advocates for centrist policies.

“What Democrats need to realize, when you win these seats, you’re in rental property. You don’t own them,” Kessler said. “You can keep them as long as you tend to them, but it just takes one bad cycle and they’re gone.”

Speaking of Gluesenkamp Perez, Kessler said “she’s carved out her own brand and she is able to survive in a hostile environment.”

“And if she needs some leeway to do it, then she needs that leeway,” he added. 

Her electoral formula has worked so far. She finished 7 points ahead of Kamala Harris, Democrats’ last presidential candidate, in 2024, winning by 3 points while Harris lost the district by 4. 

Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, said Gluesenkamp Perez correctly challenges billionaires and corporations but sometimes “undermines Democrats just for the performative sake of opposing Democrats.” 

“I view her politically like a teenager who’s developing muscles and learning how to use them,” Green said, “with an expectation that her punches will be stronger and aimed in a better direction more and more over time.”

John Braun is a military veteran, business executive and legislator

Ambulance, fire trucks and other emergency vehicles filled the parking lot at Braun Northwest, a manufacturer that sits alongside Interstate 5, the main thoroughfare through the district.

John Braun’s parents founded the business 40 years ago, and he was named president in 2006.

A retired Navy captain in the submarine service, a business executive and the Republican leader in the state Senate, Braun, 59 has the kind of pedigree that dominated his party before Trump remade it in his image. 

It’s far different from Joe Kent, the party’s nominee who lost to Gluesenkamp Perez in 2022 and 2024. Kent’s campaign team included a consultant who was a member of the Proud Boys, and Kent supported conspiracy theories about the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.

Kent went on to lead the National Counterterrorism Center under Trump, resigning in March because of opposition to the Iran war. 

Braun predicted that he would have more appeal to independent-minded voters, saying in an interview that Kent “wasn’t a good fit for the district.”

Gluesenkamp Perez has focused on “marginal issues” affecting slivers of her constituency and, despite some high-profile disputes, hasn’t broken with Democrats on “the things that really matter,” Braun said. 

“It’s a very independent district, and while I think she has said ‘independent’ a lot, there’s a lot of frustration that she really hasn’t been all that independent,” Braun said. 

Sandy Johnson, a 74-year-old Republican from Battle Ground, said Braun’s background in business is appealing, and he doesn’t see any difference between Gluesenkamp Perez and other Democrats. 

“I can’t stand her. I think she’s a liar. She’s a manipulator,” Johnson said as he walked his dog in a park near his home. “She’s directed by them, and she follows them, not us.”

news.title: The GOP Counts on Farmers’ Votes. As a Costly Harvest Season Raises Concerns, Trump Heads to Kansas
news.text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Fifth-generation Kansas farmer Glenn Brunkow describes this time of year as “go time,” when farmers are combining fields, hauling crops to town and moving livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.

But this harvest season, they’re doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits.

“It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions,” said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.

The economic strain is becoming a growing political concern for Republicans in states they have long dominated. President Donald Trump is heading to Kansas on Monday and Iowa later in the week, the latest in a series of stops where he’s trying to energize his base in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

The visits come as Republicans pour money into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa amid concerns about voter enthusiasm. The anxiety may be especially notable in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 — as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas in 94 years.

Brunkow, whose organization endorsed Marshall, said he’s been asked many times whether the economic frustrations could drive Republican farmers to vote for Democrats.

“I don’t think it necessarily does that,” Brunkow said. “But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls.”

Republican voters’ frustrations with the party have deepened
Don Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.

He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.

“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”

Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.

“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”

Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn’t seen Marshall do. She’s never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.

“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. “I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”

Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.

“And then of course the trade agreements,” she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”

Farmers face a financial squeeze
Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.

Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.

“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.

The Trump administration has attempted to ease some of those burdens. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.

Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump, although he thinks most would still consider him the better choice in the 2024 election.

“He’s made some unforced errors,” said Brunkow. “Miscalculations, bad advice, that had unintended consequences.”

Concerns spread beyond Kansas
Trump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.

In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.

David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.

“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”

Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.

Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.

“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”

A third-generation farmer, Tester said he first began farming in 1978 and witnessed the farm crisis of the 1980s, when “a fair number of my neighbors left town.”

“We’re setting up for the same kind of situation,” said Tester. “The economics in family farm production agriculture right now are probably worse right now than they were in the 1980s.”

By JOEY CAPPELLETTI and JOHN HANNA Associated Press
Cappelletti reported from Washington. Associated Press journalist Nick Ingram contributed to this report.

news.title: Harry Enten Reveals How Donald Trump Is 'History-Making' In The Worst Possible Way
news.text:
Inflation will be the central issue of the 2026 midterm elections in just over two weeks’ time, according to CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten.

And that exact issue is “what is so debilitating to this president of the United States, Donald John Trump, and could be debilitating to Republicans’ hopes,” Enten said on Sunday’s broadcast of “Laura Coates Live.”

Enten noted that Trump was reelected in 2024 in large part because of concerns over inflation, with voters trusting him more to tackle rising costs than his Democratic rival Kamala Harris, over whom he enjoyed a 7-percentage-point advantage on the issue.

But Trump’s net approval rating on inflation in a new ABC News-Washington Post poll showed him 52 percentage points underwater, Enten said.

“That is deeper than the East River, Hudson River, Harlem River, all combined. My goodness gracious,” he explained. “We are talking about a 59-point swing in the wrong direction for the president of the United States. On the most important issue of the day. “

Trump’s net approval rating on inflation is “history-making,” Enten added. “Go back to all the history books. Has any president ever been this bad? The answer is no, not at all.”

Enten said “the 25 worst net approval ratings ever on inflation” all belong to Trump and have all been recorded since the start of the Iran war, which Trump launched in February.

“In some polls we’re talking about -60 points or worse. My goodness gracious,” he added. “And in this case, the voters, the Americans, well, they are following what their pocketbooks are telling them when they go and try and get groceries, or when they try and go fill up their tanks at the gas station.”

news.title: All the races that will decide control of the US Senate
news.text:
Democrats must secure at least four additional seats in November's midterm elections to capture control of the 100-seat US Senate, where Republicans currently maintain a 53-47 majority.

That prospect appeared unlikely at the start of the year. 

However, voter frustration over rising prices and the war in Iran, alongside the unpopularity of President Donald Trump, has made several contests competitive, including in states he carried comfortably in 2024.

These critical races will determine control of the Senate:

Maine represents the primary opportunity for a Democratic pickup, as the single state featuring a Republican incumbent seeking re-election where Trump lost in 2024.

Republican Senator Susan Collins has distanced herself from Trump and refused to join Vice President JD Vance on the campaign trail in the state.

During a debate earlier this month, Collins — who voted to convict Trump after he was impeached following the January 6 insurrection — acknowledged that she isn't the president's favorite senator and said he won't be coming to Maine.

Democrats say she only votes against Trump in the Senate when it doesn't matter — such as when she voted against a sweeping tax-cut package last year after backing it in a procedural vote. 

Democrats hope voters will hold her accountable for helping confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the US Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of a federal right to abortion.

Democrats, however, have their own drama. The party's original nominee, progressive oysterman Graham Platner, was pressured into withdrawing following sexual assault allegations, forcing the state party to scramble for a new candidate. Platner has denied the allegations.

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, another progressive, emerged as Platner's replacement.

Jackson has nearly caught up to Collins on the fundraising front. He has raised $20.4 million (£15.3m) so far, with $4 million unspent as of September 30, while Collins has raised $24 million, with $5.4 million still in the bank.

Outside groups are spending heavily as well. AdImpact, a monitoring service, predicts they will spend a total of $199 million on this election — equal to $171 for every adult in the state.

Republican groups are outspending Democrats here, but most opinion polls show Jackson holding a narrow lead.

Democrat Sherrod Brown is seeking to return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024, and working-class frustration with the Iran war and rising prices may be giving him a tailwind.

This time, Brown faces US Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to replace Vance when he left office for the White House.

The Ohio race has become one of the most expensive Senate contests in the nation. AdImpact estimates Republican groups will spend $246 million on ads, while Democrats will spend $177 million. Brown has $16 million available for the final stretch, while Husted has $8.8 million.

Recent polls show Brown leading by between 1 and 8 percentage points.

Trump traveled to Alaska last week to shore up incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is facing a stiff challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US Representative.

Alaska allows voters to rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate. Voters will have four choices, including Sullivan, Peltola and another Dan Sullivan, a candidate Republicans have called a decoy in what they believe is a Democratic effort to confuse voters.

Peltola has outraised Sullivan, but the Republican enters the final stretch of the campaign with $5.1 million in the bank, compared to $3.1 million for Peltola. Outside Republican groups have spent $33 million, while Democratic groups have spent $27 million.

Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, but recent polls show Peltola leading or tied with Sullivan.

No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994. 

James Talarico, a state representative, could break the streak.

Talarico faces a historically weak Republican nominee in Attorney General Ken Paxton, but Texas is still Texas — a big, conservative-leaning state that has dashed Democratic hopes repeatedly in recent years.

Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024. Yet outside Republican groups have already spent a staggering $240 million to hold the seat after runoff voters nominated the scandal-plagued Paxton over incumbent Republican US Senator John Cornyn. 

Trump endorsed Paxton even though Cornyn was widely believed to have an easier path to victory.

Leaked audio has exposed daylight between Trump and Paxton, who privately told donors that the president's midterm convention hurt his campaign. 

Democratic groups have spent $50 million on this race, far less than Republicans. But Talarico's campaign has outraised Paxton's by $49 million and reported $16 million more in its campaign coffers as of September 30.

Opinion polls show the race ranging from a tie to a 6-point Talarico lead.

Trump's unpopularity, tariffs and the Iran war have put Republicans on defense in Iowa, where Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

Republican US Senator Joni Ernst's decision not to seek reelection has made this an open-seat contest between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist.

Hinson has called for an "immediate end" to the Iran war and said Iowans should not have to pay higher fuel or grocery prices as a result of it. However, she has repeatedly voted against resolutions in Congress calling for an end to the war.

Hinson has outraised Turek and had $6.9 million available to spend as of September 30, nearly three times what Turek has in his war chest. Outside Republican groups have spent $61 million to Democrats' $55 million.

Recent polls show the race effectively tied.

The Democratic establishment didn't get its pick in Michigan. 

Progressive outsider Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate US Representative Haley Stevens during the primary, putting him on a collision course with Republican Mike Rogers, a former US Representative, in what could be the tightest race for a Democratic-held Senate seat this year.

Rogers has said Canada is not the United States' enemy, distancing himself from the president and his tariffs.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris has campaigned with El-Sayed, and former President Barack Obama is set to rally with him later this month. The latest batch of polls shows El-Sayed leading by between 1 and 7 percentage points.

Republicans have spent $104 million in Michigan's Senate race, nearly double Democrats' $55 million.

Democrats are defending another open seat in New Hampshire, though this is a state Harris won by nearly 3 points in 2024.

Democratic US Representative Chris Pappas is running against former US Senator John Sununu, who was ousted by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. Shaheen is retiring.

Sununu benefits from a famous last name. His brother Chris was governor until last year, and his father — also named John — was a governor and White House chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush.

Republicans have outspent Democrats in this race, $30 million to $15.5 million.

Pappas has maintained a consistent polling lead of 5 to 8 points in recent surveys.

Incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff appears to be holding his own against a challenge from Republican Representative Mike Collins in Georgia, a state Trump won by 2 percentage points in 2024. Recent polls show Ossoff holding a double-digit lead, and some outside Republican groups have pulled out of the race.

Ossoff holds a clear financial advantage. He has raised $98 million as of September 30, with $26.3 million still unspent. Collins, by contrast, has raised $11 million and has $1.1 million available.

Republicans appear to have conceded North Carolina, where outside spending groups have dropped their support significantly in recent weeks.

Opinion polls show former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper holding a steady lead over former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, a Trump ally. 

It's a pickup opportunity for Democrats, as Republican Senator Thom Tillis is not seeking reelection.

Cooper has raised $47.2 million, more than three times as much as his opponent, and has $12.5 million left to spend. Whatley has less than $1 million in the bank.

Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024.

The political environment has shifted in favor of Democrats so much that Kansas is now in play. Republicans have diverted resources from North Carolina to shore up US Senator Roger Marshall, who in recent weeks has condemned the activity of Immigration and Customs Enforcement in his state.

Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024, but the state has twice elected Democratic Governor Laura Kelly. And Republican leaders have acknowledged the race is competitive and closer than they would like it to be. 

Marshall's opponent is Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of a Methodist megachurch. Marshall's campaign has outraised Hamilton's by $3 million and has nearly $1 million more unspent.

In a reversal of the usual pattern, Democratic groups have outspent Republicans here, $16 million to $11 million.

Recent polls show Hamilton leading by between 1 and 3 percentage points.

news.title: Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge
news.text:
Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI.
Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings.
AI issues are already taking a leading role in campaign ads, particularly as data center development has driven residents across the political spectrum to packed local meetings. While President Donald Trump has opposed most regulation of the technology in favor of an accelerationist approach, public opinion polling has shown that Americans have widespread concerns about how AI will impact jobs, education, and other aspects of life. The direction and intensity of that oversight, though, is up for grabs.
The issue of AI is “a hundred percent ready for the taking,” says Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist who previously ran a tech accountability advocacy group and worked for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity.” AI issues currently include a lot of different things, from monitoring and restricting the development of frontier models to dealing with the effects of job displacement or data centers’ energy demands. Across both parties, lawmakers are still figuring out where to put their stakes in the ground, and early congressional proposals have yet to gain broad consensus.
AI caught many lawmakers off guard, says Rob Flaherty, former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign and a Biden White House alum who cohosts a podcast with Lehrich. “For a long time, Democrats were afraid to talk about it, either for a mix of not understanding it, or being afraid of the money that was going to be poured in by the AI industry,” Flaherty says. But as AI becomes more salient for voters, “there will be immense profit to whoever can speak to the world that we’re moving into at a volume that voters can hear and can feel.”
Flaherty recently launched a super PAC called Tomorrow Together with Karthik Ganapathy, a former state communications director for Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign. The group launched its first $4 million ad blitz last week in battleground House races, attacking Republican candidates as out of touch on AI and referencing issues like kids’ online safety and data centers. The group is looking beyond the midterms toward the 2028 presidential election, aiming to hone Democrats’ messaging to double down on what resonates most with voters.
While data centers have been the most visible AI issue in many communities, Flaherty says his group’s polling found sweeping bans on state AI regulation — repeatedly pushed by Trump and congressional Republicans — are even more broadly unpopular. Democratic donor and venture capitalist Ron Conway now regrets funding Marc Andreessen-backed pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, Jay Carney, a former Obama press secretary who now runs communications for Conway’s VC fund, told Politico.
As of June, LTF spent nearly $45 million over almost a year, with $31 million left in the pot according to Federal Election Commission filings. “At a certain point, voters speak louder than money,” Flaherty says. Even governors who lean toward the center of the Democratic Party, like California’s Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, have taken bolder stances against AI in recent weeks. Newsom issued an executive order looking to create an AI “kill switch” after previously vetoing a bill that would have instituted some similar measures, and Shapiro reversed course against data centers.
Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI because Trump’s largely anti-regulation stance has boxed in his party. Though some Republicans, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), have carved out a more skeptical approach to AI, Lehrich says, “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry and declaring that we must let data reign and any community that rejects data centers is backwards and poor.”
A more sweeping AI regulatory agenda might include embedding independent researchers into frontier labs, requiring more safety checks up front, and imposing more liability on tech companies for anything from how their tools affect kids to whether they’re used to discriminate against workers or housing applicants. Lawmakers could also consider ways to meet demands from constituents that AI companies help pay for job displacement and other impacts they’ll have on people’s lives.
AI is still not the top issue driving voters to the polls, but Flaherty says that’s not necessarily the right way to think about it. “AI is not an issue as much as it is a story,” he says. “It’s a story of politicians getting bought off by industry. It’s a story of a bunch of guys making you foot the bill for them getting rich while they’re coming to make your life worse. It is a story that fits the national vibe.”
Where exactly different policy lines should be drawn on AI is still somewhat unsettled. But Flaherty warns that Democrats risk giving up ground if they fail to take big enough swings. Voters are “giving politicians a lot of leeway to take big swings and to really reimagine stuff,” he says. If politicians only stick to basics like plans to retrain workers at community colleges, “I think we’re going to miss the bigness and the ingenuity that the moment calls for.”

news.title: Trump’s tiny-crowd problem will hit him right in the ego
news.text:
Donald Trump has blown hot and cold on the midterm elections. Sometimes, the President doesn’t seem to care much about them at all: his name is not on the ballot, and his term will continue through to January 2029. But in the final weeks of the campaign, Trump finally seems to have become engaged with the elections – and he is suddenly facing a new, very embarrassing, problem.

In the month of October, Trump has rallied in Texas (twice), Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio (twice), Nebraska, Tennessee, Alaska, Montana, New York and Kentucky. That is a punishing schedule for an 80-year-old man also responsible for running the government of the world’s largest superpower during wartime.

But there is something else notable about that list of states: Trump won every single one of them (bar New York) by double-digit margins in the presidential general election just two years ago. Most of these states are the Republican heartlands.

But in some of them, the Republicans are in trouble. Trump beat Kamala Harris in Kansas by a margin of 16 points, but as he heads there tonight its Senate race is now a toss-up. Even Nebraska – which Trump won by 20 points – has an outside chance of electing someone who isn’t a Republican. The Republican Party is not fighting to win, so much as it is trying to make sure that its loss is merely bad, rather than devastating.

The way it is using Donald Trump plays into this. Republican strategists know that Trump is deeply unpopular in the country at large – his approval is at 32 per cent – and is mostly keeping him out of the usual swing states. The theory is that Trump can do his thing in states that are usually safely Republican, that voted for him heavily just two years ago, and hopefully can energise the remaining faithful so that they turn out to the polls.

It is a strategy that makes sense on paper, not least because it feeds into the fragile ego of Trump – a man who loves to give long, rambling speeches at rallies, and who loves to boast about the size of the audience he can pull into them.

There is one major problem, though: even in the reddest of red states, Trump rallies in 2026 seem to have a problem with empty seats.

As the camera panned around the San Antonio’s Freeman Coliseum as Trump spoke earlier this month, anyone looking at the crowd would see the upper tier was sparsely populated. Trump himself noticed from the podium, blustering to explain away the gaps like a schoolchild claiming they really did have a girlfriend, only she goes to another school. In Canada.

“Look at this place. Every corner. They will say they spotted an empty seat,” Trump said. “You know, there are lines that are two miles long outside. They can’t get in.”

Even this was better than Trump’s rally in Kentucky, a state he won by 30 points, on Saturday, where the entire upper level of the arena was left completely empty, leading the New York Times to note a comment from an anonymous staffer, who “said they had expected a larger audience than was on hand”.

Rallies are not attended by floating voters or people who vote for the lesser of two evils – the people who go to these events know that they will be queuing up for hours, will have to go through security screening and then will have to wait again for Trump to start speaking. Given Trump’s meandering speaking style, that might take hours, too.

Previously, when Trump’s approval has fallen among his less committed voters, his Maga faithful have stuck with him. Now, though, his crowds seem to be thinning out. This isn’t Trump’s first inauguration, where the President desperately pretended to have got a record-breaking crowd in the left-wing, liberal city of Washington DC.

Instead, this is Trump failing to pack out relatively small venues in deep-red states. Trump’s base stuck with him through “grab ‘em by the pussy”, through Russiagate, through election denial and January 6. Now, they seem to be losing interest.

Few things will hit Trump harder than the idea that he can’t thrill a crowd of his supporters any more – but those who wish to succeed him as president will be taking notice: if Trump can’t pack out an arena any more, perhaps the Maga coalition won’t outlive the Trump presidency, after all.

news.title: Could right-wing commentator Laura Loomer be the next White House press secretary?
news.text:
Laura Loomer, a far-right activist and vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, has put herself forward as a possible candidate for White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia’s abrupt departure from the role. Her proposal has drawn attention online, with conservative commentator Candace Owens responding with what appeared to be a sarcastic endorsement.
Loomer made her pitch on X on October 16, shortly after news emerged that Zacharia was leaving the position after only a few days. In a series of posts, Loomer argued that she would be suited to the job and promised to bring evidence to presidential briefings.
“I would be an amazing Press Secretary. I’d show President Trump all the receipts. I would bring my binder full of receipts to every briefing,” she wrote.
In another post, she suggested that changing her appearance might improve her chances of getting the job. “So you’re saying if I dye my hair blonde and I change my name to Kora I have a chance?” she asked.
The Hill reported that Loomer had put herself forward as Zacharia’s replacement as the White House communications team faced another shake-up.
What did Candace Owens say about Loomer’s pitch?
Owens reacted to Loomer’s proposal on October 17 with a series of posts that appeared to use irony to question the prospect of her appointment.
“I FULLY endorse this. Every person who understands the Bolshevik takeover of this country should support this. Laura Loomer representing Donald Trump and MAGA is the catalyst our country needs,” Owens wrote.
She followed it with another message, “We need her hired and the neocons defending her hiring. Let’s go!”
I FULLY endorse this.
Every person who understands the Bolshevik takeover of this country should support this.
Laura Loomer representing Donald Trump and MAGA is the catalyst our country needs.
We need her hired and the neocons defending her hiring.
Let’s go! 🔥
— Candace Owens (@RealCandaceO) October 17, 2026
Owens’ remarks appeared to be sarcastic rather than a straightforward expression of support. However, her comments added to the online debate about Loomer’s ambitions and the changing White House press team.
Owens also commented on Zacharia’s departure. Sharing a Lionel Media post on X, she wrote, “I’m going to miss her.”
The contrast between the two reactions attracted attention, particularly as Loomer herself had defended the outgoing press secretary against criticism.
In a separate post, Loomer said people were being “unnecessarily cruel” to Zacharia. She described the outgoing press secretary as someone who appeared to want to serve Trump and argued that public scrutiny had been excessive.
“I wish Katie the best,” Loomer wrote. “I think it’s great that President Trump has people who are so devoted to his cause they are willing to subject themselves to public nitpicking on a daily basis. I’m sure he appreciates it and I think Katie had good intentions.”
She also defended Zacharia’s nervousness during her first briefing, and wrote, “She was nervous. It’s not a crime.”
Loomer added that the criticism should stop, and added, “Just leave her alone now. The continued dogpiling is just malicious. Let her be.”
Why did Katie Zacharia leave the role?
Zacharia’s departure followed a brief and difficult introduction to the White House press briefing room. Trump announced her appointment on October 9, describing her as a longtime supporter with an “unblemished record of support”.
He also said she would “work fantastically with the Media, the American People, and my Administration”.
She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down at the end of August following the birth of her second child.
Zacharia’s first briefing on Tuesday lasted around 14 minutes, during which she took questions from only three media outlets. Her performance attracted criticism over its brevity, her delivery and her reliance on prepared remarks.
 Katie Zacharia’s tenure as White House press secretary ended after just five days, following criticism of her first briefing and scrutiny over her legal qualifications. File image/Reuters
Her professional qualifications also came under scrutiny after Trump described her as an attorney. According to Hindustan Times, Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011 but did not pass the California bar examination.
She later told Fox News host Sean Hannity that she had taken the exam once and failed, adding that the result was “inconsequential” because she expected to move to China.
A White House official told Newsweek that Zacharia was “transitioning” out of the position, while CNN, citing presidential advisers, reported that Trump had fired her.
Trump subsequently told reporters that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider the role. “I just asked her, ‘Is this for you?’” he said. “And she’s a nice person. I’m going to let her make that decision.”
He also said the media had treated her “very, very unfairly” and that she was being “brutalized by the media”. “I told her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I would reconsider,’” Trump said. “Maybe it’s not for her.”
The rapid exit has left the White House looking for another press secretary, although Trump said he was not in a hurry to fill the vacancy.
Who is Laura Loomer, and could she get the job?
Loomer is a controversial far-right activist and conspiracy theorist who has maintained close ties with Trump. She has frequently appeared at events supporting him and has previously travelled on his plane.
In an April 4, 2025 report, BBC News examined Loomer’s influence on Trump after reports that she had urged him to dismiss National Security Council officials she considered insufficiently loyal. Trump denied that she had played any role in the firings.
“I don’t control Laura. Laura has to say what she wants. She’s a free spirit,” Trump said previously, describing her as “just a supporter”.
Loomer has faced criticism from Republicans over her rhetoric and conspiracy theories. She has promoted baseless claims, including that the US government was involved in the September 11 attacks. She also attracted condemnation for comments about immigrants and Kamala Harris.
In 2024, Republican Senator Thom Tillis wrote on X. “Laura Loomer is a crazy conspiracy theorist who regularly utters disgusting garbage intended to divide Republicans.”
Marjorie Taylor Greene, another Trump supporter, also criticised Loomer’s remarks about Harris, calling them “appalling and extremely racist” and saying they did “not represent who we are as Republicans or MAGA”.
Despite the controversy, Loomer has continued to present herself as a committed Trump supporter and has previously attracted attention for her proximity to the president. The BBC reported in April 2025 that she had met Trump amid questions about her influence on his decisions.
Other potential candidates for the press secretary position have also been discussed. The Hill reported that Anna Kelly, the White House deputy press secretary, and conservative commentator Scott Jennings were among those previously considered to replace Leavitt.
White House communications director Steven Cheung and conservative author Elizabeth Pipko have also been mentioned in reports.
Prediction market Kalshi listed Jennings as the leading contender on October 16, followed by Kelly and Pipko.

news.title: Our two-party system is broken. Independents like me know it
news.text:
Editor's note: This column is part of Changing Minds, a USA TODAY Opinion series. Ahead of the November midterm elections, we talked with people who changed their political beliefs after years of seeing things a certain way. We'll publish their stories over the next few days.

Don't look now, but the 2026 midterms are weeks away. Weeks. Two years of President Donald Trump's second term have sped by, and there has been so much news and partisan warfare that one group is easy to ignore.

Independent voters. 

So we decided to include you, wonderful people, in a series of columns dedicated to the idea that people can, and sometimes do, change their minds. We visited a Texas border community, heard from a mother wrestling with her idea of what marriage is, and even spoke with somebody who took part in the riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. (Check back here for those pieces.)

Here, though, we're showcasing a second round of responses we got in our Opinion Forum from asking independent voters how they feel.

Want to share your perspective? Weigh in at usatoday.com/forum or drop us a note at forum@usatoday.com.

I changed my mind on the president, but not the two-party system

I'm now an independent. I was a Republican until the bailout of 2008 or whenever. Although I'm an independent, I voted for President Donald Trump. I now think he should be impeached. But that doesn't mean I'm a Democrat. The Democratic Party is just as bad or worse in some ways than the Republican Party. It's sad that we say we have freedom and a choice. We don't. Rich, power-hungry person A or rich, power-hungry person B. I'm so sick of it. Every single congressman should be voted out.

Do Republicans and Democrats represent Americans? Well, they manipulate and divide their followers. They represent a minority of Americans but yet have all the power. I do believe a third party system is possible and desperately needed.

- Kevin Harbolt, Missouri

Independent voters are America's moderate middle

I identify as an independent voter because I don't feel like I belong in either party. I was a Republican from the time I signed up to vote, from 2007 to 2015. I worked in the Republican Party and believed I would be a part of the party for a long time. But in 2016, after then-Sen. Marco Rubio lost the presidential primary in Florida, I became an independent. I thought about becoming a Democrat, but I do not agree with all the policies of the Democratic Party and feel most at home in the moderate middle, with other like-minded independents.

Independents are shut out of primaries, which is where the majority of our congressional elections are decided. If independents are to have true representative voting power, then we need to have open primaries for all voters.

With the "spoiler effect," independents nowadays can make or break an election, but so often when they run for office they are seen as a "spoiler" to the traditional two-party system. If Americans are truly to vote their conscience, Americans need more options.

I believe the majority of Americans agree on more things than they disagree on, and the majority are moderates. It is the two-party system and the 24-hour entertainment news cycle that have pushed electoral politics to the extreme. 

I believe reaching out to unaffiliated voters is the right approach and will bring the temperature of politics down. When the candidate only has to speak to their base, the most extreme candidate wins, but when a candidate must communicate with those whose views might differ slightly, they are encouraged to find common ground.

People are leaving the Democratic and Republican parties in droves because they do not feel properly represented. They are voting with their feet, telling us that they want another option because their options do not fit them anymore. I strongly believe a multiparty system would encourage greater dialogue and force representatives to work together for the will of the citizens over the dollar of the largest donor.

- Caroline Anderson, Florida

America's two-party system is long outdated

I am registered as an independent voter. In the past, I was a Democrat, then a Republican. I turned independent when I saw parallels between how bad the two parties are for the citizens.

Both sides consider us easy to manipulate. They label us "fence-riders." We are not. We dare to see what they do not. That both sides are too power-hungry. And that they make promises they don't plan to keep.

What needs to happen is that individual candidates need to be as transparent as possible. I don't care what party you are from; if your campaign views mesh with mine, then I will vote for you.

The two-party system is old and outdated. Quit dogmatically voting based on what party you are affiliated with and base your votes on the individual candidate and their views or campaign promises. Plus, their campaigns are based on "keywords," not ideas, principles or substance.

- Kavian Darkain, Pennsylvania 

There are more moderates than MAGAs 

I am a registered independent. I registered as a Republican in 1979. I changed to become a Democrat after the recession of 2008 and the rise of the Tea Party movement. I changed to independent around 2022. I believe that both parties are ruled by extremists, and that the only way to get back to a moderate government is to open primaries to all registered voters. Not just the two main parties.

Independents have too little influence due to closed primaries like in my state, Kentucky. But I believe that in time our influence will increase as more people register as independents.

It has been said that we need to just pick a party so we can participate in elections. I don't agree with that opinion. Why should I settle for a political party that I believe caters to its extreme elements?

I think the Democratic Party is trying to appeal to nonaffiliated voters, but I don't see the Republicans doing that. It's MAGA or nothing. That isn't a very effective strategy, because there are more moderates than MAGAs.

- Katherine Boswell, Kentucky

Independents aren't swing voters. We're our own faction

I became an independent voter shortly before the last election. I had been a lifelong Democrat previously. I am 56, and I voted a mixed ticket last election, voting for Kamala Harris for president. If I had to do it over again, I would now vote for Trump in that election.

I think it was, for me, the deception of the Democratic Party and the BBC editing of footage of Trump's speech on Jan. 6, 2021, which seems designed to mislead the populace.

I think increasingly, independent voters are becoming a third faction with their own specific ideology based upon honesty, authenticity, common sense and logic. And a rejection of identity politics. I think they need much more power.

I think people believe that independent voters are simply left- or right-wing-leaning people who reject labels. What I'm seeing now is a comprehensive third way forward that the American populist is starting to embrace.

The financial constraints that prevented parties from competing are largely disappearing as social media, artificial intelligence, video production and other tools make reaching the public much more about messaging than financing. 

One of the biggest blocks has been registering a party's candidates in all 50 states, something the Libertarian Party has already done. Most independent voters tend to have libertarian leanings, as far as I can see. At the same time, most of them are not stalwart libertarian voters. But the Libertarian Party can easily be reformed. The other two parties cannot.

- David Levine, Oregon
