news.text: Millions of Americans will head to the polls on November 3 for the 2026 midterm elections, but for many, voting will be over before Election Day. Early voting is already underway in several states, with start dates as early as mid-September, while Texas is among the next states to open early voting, with polling locations set to open Monday. The map highlights the different timelines voters face as states prepare for the November 3 election. The schedule comes amid an intensifying national debate over voting access, election security and President Donald Trump's efforts to change how Americans cast ballots ahead of contests that will determine control of Congress. Early Voting Kicks Off in Texas, Four Other States on Monday Texas will begin early in-person voting on Monday giving registered voters until October 30 to cast their ballots before Election Day, according to the Texas Secretary of State. Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado and Connecticut are also listed as beginning early voting on October 19 in Ballotpedia's 2026 calendar. South Carolina is scheduled to start the same day. The dates come as campaigns across the country intensify their efforts to mobilize voters in races that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Where Has Early Voting Already Started? Early voting has already begun in a number of states, with schedules varying across the country. Minnesota, South Dakota and Virginia were among the earliest to begin, with voting starting September 18. Vermont followed on September 19, while Illinois began on September 24. Several more states opened early voting in October. California, Maine, Montana and Nebraska were listed with October 5 start dates, followed by Indiana, New Mexico, Ohio and Wyoming on October 6. Arizona began on October 7. Georgia and Idaho opened early voting on October 13, while Iowa, Kansas, Rhode Island and Tennessee were scheduled to begin on October 14. Texas, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado and Connecticut all open early voting today. Oregon primarily conducts elections by mail, while North Dakota and Pennsylvania have schedules that vary by jurisdiction. Early Voting Coming Soon in Delaware, Florida and Other States Beyond the October 19 openings, several states will begin early voting in the final two weeks before Election Day. Hawaii, Louisiana and Utah are listed as starting on October 20, followed by West Virginia on October 21. Delaware and Maryland are scheduled to begin on October 22. Florida, Michigan, New Jersey and New York are listed with October 24 start dates, while the District of Columbia is scheduled to begin on October 26. Oklahoma follows on October 28, with Kentucky starting October 29. Voters should check their state or local election office for precise dates, polling locations and operating hours. In some states, early in-person voting dates differ from deadlines for requesting or returning mail ballots. Highly Contested Midterm Races The early voting calendar is unfolding alongside competitive contests that could determine control of the House and Senate. In the Senate, races in Georgia, Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska and Texas are among those attracting attention. Texas is drawing particular interest as Republicans defend a seat in a state that has long favored the party in statewide elections. The House map is also in flux. Both parties are adjusting campaign spending across competitive districts, with strategists reassessing where resources could make the greatest difference. With early voting opening at different times across the country, campaigns have limited windows to reach voters before ballots are cast. The November 3 results will determine the balance of power in Congress and shape the legislative landscape for the rest of Trump's presidency. Senate Races to Watch Georgia: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is seeking reelection against Republican Representative Mike Collins. Ossoff has built a substantial fundraising advantage, and recent polls cited by Reuters have shown him leading by double digits. The race is a key Democratic priority as Republicans seek to defend their Senate majority. Michigan: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is competing against former Republican Representative Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat. El-Sayed narrowly won his party's primary against Representative Haley Stevens, while Rogers has sought to distinguish himself from Trump's tariff policies. Recent polls have shown a close contest, with outside groups spending heavily on both sides. Maine: Republican Senator Susan Collins faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson. Collins has sought to establish distance from Trump on some issues while maintaining support for key Republican legislative priorities. Democrats see the race as an opportunity to gain a seat in a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024, though the party's nomination process has added complications to the contest. North Carolina: Democrat Roy Cooper, the state's former governor, is running against Republican Michael Whatley for an open Senate seat. Cooper has maintained a polling lead in surveys cited by Reuters, while Republican groups have spent heavily on the race. Ohio: Democrat Sherrod Brown, a former senator, is attempting to reclaim a seat against Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed after JD Vance left the Senate to become vice president. Trump carried Ohio by a double-digit margin in 2024, but recent polling has shown a competitive race. The contest has also attracted substantial outside spending. Texas: Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994. Paxton won the Republican nomination over incumbent Senator John Cornyn, despite concerns among some Republicans about his prospects in the general election. Talarico has outraised Paxton, and recent polls have shown a close contest. Republicans have committed substantial resources to defending the seat. Alaska: Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola. Although Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, recent polls have shown Peltola leading or running close to Sullivan. Alaska's ranked-choice voting system adds another dimension to the contest, in which voters rank candidates in order of preference. Other races, including contests in New Hampshire, Iowa and Kansas, are also drawing attention as the parties reassess their paths to a Senate majority. Trump’s Changing Position on Mail-in Voting As early voting gets underway across the country ahead of the November midterms, Trump has repeatedly criticized one of its main alternatives: voting by mail. He has called mail-in ballots fraudulent and pledged to end the practice, while continuing to make unsubstantiated claims that alleged fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. At a White House event in August 2025, Trump vowed to eliminate mail ballots, saying: “We as a Republican Party are going to do everything possible that we get rid of mail-in ballots ... because they're corrupt.” “We're going to end mail-in voting. It's a fraud,” he added. On March 31, Trump sought to expand the federal government's role in elections, signing an executive order directing federal agencies to compile citizenship verification lists and instructing the U.S. Postal Service to pursue new rules governing mail-in and absentee ballots. The administration said the measures were intended to strengthen election security and prevent ineligible voting. The order did not abolish early in-person voting but sought to change aspects of how mail ballots are distributed and handled. Critics argued that the measures could burden eligible voters and encroach on states' authority to administer elections. The administration's efforts subsequently faced legal challenges. In September, the Supreme Court declined to allow the Postal Service to enforce the proposed restrictions ahead of the midterms, Reuters reported. But as the November 3 elections approach, Trump's messaging has shifted. On October 5, he acknowledged that Republicans could vote by mail, despite his longstanding opposition to the practice. “They can vote by mail if they want, because we seem to have no choice because a lot of people want to vote by mail,” he told reporters at the White House, according to Reuters. The remarks contrast with his previous calls to eliminate mail-in voting. Discouraging the practice could also limit options for Republican voters who rely on it, including some rural residents and people who have difficulty reaching polling place. What Voters Should Know Early voting remains governed by state and local rules. Start dates, polling locations, operating hours, identification requirements and mail-ballot deadlines vary across the country. A statewide start date does not necessarily mean every county or municipality opens its polling locations on the same day. Some states also distinguish between early in-person voting and absentee or mail-in voting. Voters should consult their state or local election office for the rules and deadlines that apply to them. As early voting gets underway, the dispute over election security, voting access and federal authority is adding another point of contention ahead of the November 3 midterms.
news.summary: Early voting is underway in many states across the U.S. ahead of the November midterms.

news.title: Independent voters will decide the midterms. Who are they?
news.text:
Editor's note: This column is part of Changing Minds, a USA TODAY Opinion series. Ahead of the November midterm elections, we talked with people who changed their political beliefs after years of seeing things a certain way. We'll publish their stories over the next few days.

This year's midterm elections narrative casts those contests as a tug-of-war across the political spectrum, pitting enthusiasm-driven Democrats against Republicans eager to retain control of Congress.

But one large and growing block of voters goes overlooked in that telling, probably because they make far less political noise than democratic socialists on the left and President Donald Trump's MAGA base on the right.

Independent voters will decide the midterms. They usually do.

Independents can be challenging to define, as they have never been one homogeneous, like-minded group and come to their place on the voter rolls from different paths. So who are they?

Independent voters are the hardest voting block to understand

Joshua Dyck, a professor of political science at The University of Massachusetts Lowell, told me that independent voters break into two groups when questioned with a seven-point party identification scale, which measures attachment to a political party.

Two-thirds of independent voters actually lean toward the Democratic Party or the Republican Party as reliable partisan voters 80-85% of the time, Dyck said.

The rest – the professor called them "pure independents" – dislike politics and don't engage with the process. They cast their ballots based on "lived experience" in their personal lives, not partisan rhetoric. And he said pure independents can be three times more likely to not vote in elections.

The American National Elections Studies, a collaboration of four universities and funded by the National Science Foundation, set the number of "pure independents" or "independent independents" at just 6.7% of the electorate during the 2024 presidential election, based on the seven-point party identification scale.

Gallup's quarterly survey of party affiliation found that in the third quarter of 2026, 45% of Americans identified as independents while 30% called themselves Democrats and 25% identified as Republicans.

Ken Goldstein, a professor of politics at the University of San Francisco, told me that "there is probably no more profoundly confusing group than independents, because you're really putting lots of sorts of people in there." And, Goldstein said, it can be challenging to compare independent voting trends from election to election "because people will go in and out of that group."

What impact have independents had on federal elections?

Independent voters have tilted toward Democratic candidates in four of the past five federal election cycles for president and Congress from 2016 to 2024. And Trump appears to be a factor in which way they swing.

Independents helped Trump edge Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential election, leaning his way by 4 percentage points. That marked the beginning of the end for Trump and independents, who swung toward Democrats running for Congress by a margin of 54% to 42% over Republicans, in the middle of his first term.

Democrats picked up 41 House seats in 2018, thanks in part to voter concerns about economic issues and Trump.

Independents helped defeat Trump in the 2020 presidential election, with 54% supporting Joe Biden to 41% for Trump. The margins were much closer in the middle of Biden's term, with independents favoring Democrats in congressional races by just 2 percentage points.

The backing of independents was not enough to help Kamala Harris head off Trump's return to office in the 2024 election, when they favored her over him by 3 points.

Experts say independents won't help Republicans in midterms

The trend of independents backing Democrats looks likely to continue when Election Day arrives on Nov. 3. A New York Times/Sienna Poll released Sept. 14 asked independent voters if they lean toward a political party: 57% said they favor Democrats, while 33% said Republicans and 10% did not know or would not say.

Larry Sabato, director of the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, told me he has seen projections that independent voters this year lean as hard as 70% to Democrats, compared with 30% to Republicans. He added that those numbers "realistically" will be closer to 60-40% on Election Day.

Democrats, Sabato told me in an email, "are enthusiastic and angry," while Republicans are mostly sticking with Trump, and he expects turnout for those voters to be down on Election Day. And independents?

"Independents seem to have had their fill of Trump, and the Iran war, and high gas/diesel prices, and grocery costs, and corruption," Sabato said. "It's one of the reasons Republicans are not going to do terribly well in the end."

A Sept. 15 Economist/YouGov poll showed that 54% of self-identified independent voters would support a Democratic candidate for Congress in a generic ballot survey, while just 27% leaned Republican and 19% were not sure.

A midterm ballot tracker compiled by Morning Consult shows Democrats up 15 percentage points with independent voters, a 12-point shift since Trump started his second term in January 2025.

Goldstein noted that so many elections are being decided by narrow margins because there are "vanishingly few number of people who changed their minds from election to election." That makes motivating independents, especially those who have swung Republican in the past, so important.

"If I'm a Democrat and I get a Democrat out to vote, that's plus one," Goldstein said. "If I'm a Republican and I get a Republican out to vote, that's plus one. If I get someone to vote for me who voted for the other side the last time, that's plus two. Because it's minus one from the other side and plus one for me."

Dyck told me that midterms are about motivated voters, and that independent voters who lean Democrat are "energized" while independents who lean Republican are not.

"I think we're going to see a big turnout surge among independents who lean towards the Democratic Party," Dyck said. "Leaning Republicans are not as energized ... because they control the reins of government right now. When you govern, it also gives you more things to be angry at your party about, especially if you're ... just weakly attached."

All signs point to voters being angry. Democrats will benefit from that

The notion of voter anger kept coming up as I did interviews for this column. 

Chad Peace, legal adviser for the Independent Voter Project, a nonprofit that advocates for allowing independent voters to cast ballots in primary elections, said Trump capitalized on voter anger in 2016 and 2024. He called Trump "the bull in the China shop" at a time when voters felt their elected officials had failed them.

"And now there's some people going, you know what, I don't like this administration either," Peace said. "The shoe is on the other foot because the administration that was the rebels, so to speak, is now the institution. People are starting to wake up to the reality that we didn't end up with better representation."

Independent voters, Peace added, will end up in the midterms "where their vote is going to send the biggest message that they're unsatisfied."

Democrats are enthusiastic and angry. Republicans seem demoralized and wary. Independents, known for moving around on the political spectrum, seem headed steadfastly in one direction this year – toward Democratic candidates.

The polling and the experts I spoke to are in sync – independent voters will bring to the midterm ballot a serious sense of dissatisfaction that will swing the midterms away from Trump and the Republicans.

news.title: CNN Data Guru Hits Trump With ‘Debilitating’ Reality
news.text:
CNN data guru Harry Enten has handed Donald Trump a painful reality check about the issue that helped put him back in the White House.

With just over two weeks left before the midterms, the network’s chief data analyst was asked on Sunday night’s Laura Coates Live to test the president’s claims that he has brought inflation down. 

“With 16 days to go, Trump keeps suggesting inflation is under control and what we’re entering is the golden age. Problem is, the numbers have just been quite a bit different,” host Laura Coates said.

CNN has repeatedly fact-checked the 80-year-old president’s rosy inflation figures on the campaign trail. Trump has repeatedly insisted inflation is coming down, including at rallies in Ohio, Alaska, and Montana last week. But the Consumer Price Index report released Wednesday showed inflation climbing to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, driven largely by soaring gas prices. 

Enten served his verdict cold. 

“Each election has a name of the game… what this election will be determined by,” Enten said. “In this one, it is cost, cost, cost. It is inflation. And inflation is what is so debilitating to this President of the United States, Donald John Trump, and could be debilitating to Republicans’ hopes this midterm election.”

The president rode to victory on voters’ anger over prices in 2024, according to CBS News. On inflation, Americans trusted him over Kamala Harris by 7 points in the weeks before that election, Enten noted.

The 38-year-old added that Trump’s net approval on the issue now sits 52 points underwater, citing an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, marking a 59-point swing in the wrong direction. 

“That is deeper than the East River, Hudson River, Harlem River all combined,” Enten said. “My goodness gracious.”

Enten then went further, arguing that Trump has been where no president has been before. When it comes to inflation, Trump takes the cake, holding all 25 of the worst net approval ratings on inflation ever recorded. All of them have come since he launched his war on Iran in February.

“Has any president ever been this bad?” Enten asked. 

“The answer is no, not at all.”

Citing USA Facts, Enten said year-on-year inflation stood at 3 percent when Trump’s second term began and had cooled to 2.4 percent by February 2026, shortly before the war started. As of September, it is back up to 3.7 percent.

Paychecks are no longer keeping pace either. At the start of Trump’s term, wages were growing at 3.7 percent, ahead of prices. Wage growth is now 3.6 percent, trailing just behind inflation, Enten said, citing USA Facts. 

“The voters, the Americans… are following what their pocketbooks are telling them when they go and try and get groceries or when they try and go fill up their tanks at the gas station,” Enten said.

Trump is no fan of CNN. He has regularly sparred with the network’s Kaitlan Collins, and last month he banned CNN from the White House for five days, along with MS NOW and POLITICO, until a federal judge temporarily blocked the move.

On Sunday, however, Trump reposted an old Enten segment touting his popularity among Republicans, drawn from a CNN/SSRS survey from May.

The new ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll Enten cited paints a far bleaker picture. It put Trump’s overall approval at 33 percent, a record low across both his terms, with roughly three in four Americans disapproving of how he has handled inflation and the cost of living.

Enten has delivered a string of grim forecasts for the president this month. He has shown Trump sinking 36 points underwater with millennials and shedding support among the immigrant voters who helped get him over the line in 2024. 

The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment.

“The data is driving the voters,” Enten said.

CNNCNN data guru Harry Enten has handed Donald Trump a painful reality check about the issue that helped put him back in the White House.

With just over two weeks left before the midterms, the network’s chief data analyst was asked on Sunday night’s Laura Coates Live to test the president’s claims that he has brought inflation down. 

“With 16 days to go, Trump keeps suggesting inflation is under control and what we’re entering is the golden age. Problem is, the numbers have just been quite a bit different,” host Laura Coates said.

news.title: Online anti-Indian hate surges in US ahead of midterms, fuelling fears of real-world violence
news.text:
The Indian and Indian American community in the United States is under siege, facing rising online racial abuse, growing hostility towards India and a series of immigration measures that have disrupted work and student visa pathways.
Those concerns intensified this week following reports of a foiled attack on a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago. The suspect, described by authorities as a white supremacist, reportedly told a colleague that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian” people.
At the root of this racist antipathy is the proliferation of anti-Indian posts that have attracted tens of millions — perhaps hundreds of millions of views — which is increasing animosity toward the community.
With a cold and unsympathetic White House that has often not condemned the negative portrayal of the community, and lax Internet laws with no consequences for spreading hate, the more than five million people of Indian origin in the US today likely feel they are more targeted than even the beleaguered Latino community.
A report by the Washington, DC-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), a nonpartisan nonprofit, examined anti-South Asian hate on X, formerly Twitter, and three platforms popular among far-right extremists: 4chan, 8kun and Gab. The study covered January 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
The results are stunning: as of January 2025, posts solely emphasizing anti-Indian hate and racism on X itself had drawn a staggering 138.54 million views.
CSOH also noted that more than half a million hateful posts targeting South Asians appeared on X between January 2025 and June 2026. Monthly volume was 75 per cent higher in June 2026 than in January 2025, and 240 per cent higher than in January 2024. The report also identified 397,522 hateful mentions across 4chan, 8chan, and Gab in 2025. The hate propaganda would also explain the findings of a Carnegie Endowment survey, which found that one in four Indian Americans had faced racism and hate in 2025.
“The culture of hate on X exemplifies the hypocrisy of (Elon) Musk’s alleged commitment to “free speech absolutism,” noted CSOH, in a new report.
 Online ethnic slurs against the Indian community abound, including ‘pajeet’, which first originated on 4chan in 2015, mocking open defecation in India. It has expanded to other derogatory slurs like ‘latrinas’, for Indian women. The CSOH report noted that stereotypes about hygiene, immigration, employment, and race have spawned variants like “poojeet,” “shitjeet,” and “migajeet’, and feminized forms, including “pajeeta” and “poojeeta.”
The viral slurs and memes have not spared even top Republican figures like Usha Vance, the wife of the Vice President JD Vance. Far-right influencer Nick Fuentes called Usha Vance a “jeet,” and refused to apologise despite a sharp rebuke by the Vice President. Other top Republicans like Kash Patel, the FBI Director, and billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, now running for Governor of Ohio, have also been in the targets of racial vitriol.
It’s not helped the community that President Trump, too, has derided the community.
Earlier this year, Trump reposted the transcript and video of radio host Michael Savage’s podcast where he described Indians as “gangsters with laptops” who have “stepped on our flag”. Stephen Miller, key architect of the anti-immigration drive in the Trump administration, has also accused India of “cheating on immigration policies.” Another blatant dig at the community came recently, when the US Department of Education shared a post on X with the caption “Make Football Great Again,” which seemed an endorsement of a racist post by Texas Republican Bo French in which he lamented the presence of a group of Indian American fans at a University of Texas Austin football game.
A noticeable trend in hateful and incendiary posts against the community is a sharp increase when the Trump administration announces immigration restrictions, as well as when videos emerge of religious practice of Indians, especially in Texas. However, the one overriding theme of the racist posts is to Make America White Again, or the “remigration” or “Great Replacement Theory.”
The Executive Director of CSOH, Raqib Naik, in a comment to Firstpost, talked about the overwhelming number of posts that “echoed” the ‘Great Replacement Theory’.
“The most striking and frightening aspect is how pervasive invasion and replacement narratives have become. Almost half of the hate we found echoed the ‘Great Replacement’ conspiracy theory. It is the glue that binds extremist movements together and one of the most potent weapons white supremacist groups use to radicalise people,” Naik, who also serves as a Fellow at the Political Conflict, Gender, and People’s Rights Initiative at the University of California, Berkeley, said.
Naik added: “It has played a role in some of the most horrific terror attacks on minority and vulnerable communities over the past two decades. What happened in Illinois (the failed massacre at the Hindu temple) cannot be seen in isolation from the anti-Indian and anti-South Asian hate we are seeing online.”
A key element of the hate spewed online is also to subvert and marginalise the success stories of the prosperous Indian community. Posts portraying the community as invaders, job thieves, and a demographic threat made up 45 per cent of anti-South Asian hate on X, with H-1B visas and immigration serving as major drivers, CSOH noted.
Documentary-style videos alleging an Indian “invasion” have emerged as another means of manufacturing purported evidence for the narrative that the community is “taking over” America, the report said. Frontlines TPUSA, an outlet of Turning Point USA, published a documentary titled “The Indian and Muslim Takeover of Texas” on X on April 2, 2026, which received more than 900,000 views as of September 2026.
Popular influencer Tyler Oliveira, who has 9.66 million subscribers on YouTube and 426,000 followers on X, posted earlier this year a nearly hour-long documentary titled “I Exposed Texas’ Indian Invasion” on YouTube. As of September 2026, it had received 3.2 million views on YouTube and 4.2 million views on X.
The CSOH report also pointed out that South Asians are literally demonized, routinely referred to as “demon worshippers” and Indian deities depicted in abusive and racist terms. The Christian community, too, from India is not accepted and treated as outsiders.
Some racist posts go further, calling for South Asian places of worship, including the Hanuman Temple in Frisco, Texas, to be destroyed or removed and replaced with supposedly “American” monuments.
As anti-Indian rhetoric spreads online, community leaders are debating how best to respond — and whether stronger platform accountability, public advocacy or political engagement offers the most effective solution.
Sree Sreenivasan, a tech entrepreneur and former Chief Digital Officer of the Met Museum and later of New York City, told Firstpost that the way to counter the online hatred against the Indian community is to voice outrage.
“Speaking up, speaking out and pushing back is the only formula that works in the current political and media landscape. Highlighting the community's contributions at local, state and national levels is critical,” Sreenivasan said. “Online hatred can turn into IRL actions all too quickly. As we see from the foiled plot against the Hindu temple in the Chicago suburbs, we cannot take the potential threats lightly.”
Sanjyot Dunung, CEO & Founder of Atma Global and former Congressional candidate from Illinois, said the best way to counter the online hatred was to hold tech companies accountable as well as with “personal responsibility.”
“We need to hold technology companies accountable for how their platforms amplify disinformation and hate. Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act has historically provided broad liability protections for tech companies for any content posted by users. Those protections deserve serious reconsideration, particularly when algorithms actively determine what people see and amplify inflammatory content,” Dunung told Firstpost.
Dunung also cautioned against amplifying online content.
“We also need perspective. Hate crimes are real and must be taken seriously, but we should distinguish between actual increases in violence and the online amplification of every hateful incident. The FBI recorded 10,881 reported hate crime incidents in 2025, with incidents declining 7 per cent from 2024 in its comparable-agency dataset. That's still far too many, but it reminds us to examine the evidence rather than assume every viral incident represents a national trend,” Dunung said.
Republican Ritesh Tandon, the US Congressional candidate, from District 17, in California, who is pitted against the incumbent Congressman Democrat Ro Khanna, when asked if campaigning as a GOP candidate was a balancing act, in the face of online hatred that is everywhere, responded that “it isn’t a balancing act at all.”
Tandon told Firstpost: “The Republican Party stands for what Indian American families believe in: hard work, merit, family, faith and the rule of law.”
Tandon said he has been targeted “many times by the far left”.
“I don’t stay quiet. I answer with facts, I answer publicly, and I never let a lie stand, because silence is what bullies count on. And let me be clear: hate against any Indian American is wrong, whether it’s aimed at Usha Vance, Vivek Ramaswamy, Kash Patel or Kamala Harris. Our community is strongest when we stand up for each other,” Tandon said.
(By arrangement with The American Bazaar.)

news.title: Democrats remain clear favourites to gain control of Congress at midterms
news.text:
With just over two weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats have a three in four chance to gain control of the Senate, and remain overwhelming favourites to gain control of the House of Representatives in Nate Silver’s forecast model.

Democrats lead Republicans by 9.6 points on the generic ballot, and Donald Trump’s net approval is -22.3.

If disruption caused by the Iran war continues until the midterm elections, with increased petrol prices and inflation, Republicans are likely to lose control of both the House and the Senate, perhaps with huge losses.

With the oil price surging recently, petrol prices are likely to increase again before the midterms.

Trump’s ratings

In Silver’s aggregate of US national polls, Trump’s net approval is -22.3. Currently, 59.8% disapprove of his performance and 37.6% approve. There haven’t been many polls taken since Trump’s October 9 announcement of a diesel import deal with Russia.

Trump’s net approval was -22.5 in my October 7 article, but fell to a record low of -23.9 on October 9 before a slight recovery. His net approval had improved to -18.7 on September 4 before falling back.

Trump’s net approval is below what any past president since Harry Truman had at this point in their term, with Joe Biden the closest at -11.7.

On four issues tracked by Silver, Trump’s net approval is -11.6 on immigration, -30.6 on trade, -32.9 on the economy and -48.9 on inflation. Since my October 7 article, Trump’s net approval on trade has dropped two points, but has improved one point on immigration.

Silver also has an aggregate of US support for the Iran war. Currently, 56.2% are opposed to the Iran war while 35.2% support it, for a net support of -21.0, up from a record low of -27.9 in my October 7 article. 

Midterm elections on November 3

All 435 federal House of Representatives seats and 35 of the 100 senators will be up for election at November 3 midterm elections.

In 2024 elections, Republicans won the House by 220–215 over Democrats and the Senate by 53–47. Owing to Vice President JD Vance’s potential tie-breaking vote, Democrats need at least a four-seat gain to win Senate control.

As I previously wrote, owing to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats need at least a four-point margin in the generic ballot to have a good chance to win the House majority. The Senate is more skewed to Republicans as every state has two senators. Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win the Senate on a uniform swing.

In Silver’s midterm election forecast model, the generic ballot gives Democrats a 51.3–41.7 lead over Republicans, a 9.6-point margin (up from 9.2 points last Wednesday, but the same 9.6 points as in my October 7 article). Democrats’ lead had dropped to 7.4 points on September 4.

Polls that screen for likely voters usually give Democrats larger leads than polls that ask registered voters. Democrats are more likely to vote at lower turnout elections like the midterms than Republicans, when Trump is not on the ballot.

Silver’s model gives Democrats a 75% chance to win the Senate and a 94% chance to win the House, respectively 74% and 93% on October 7. Democratic chances to win the Senate had fallen to a low of 50% on September 7, and their chances of winning the House had dropped to 81% on September 3.

While uniform swing indicates that Democrats need a double-digit margin in the generic ballot to win control of the Senate, Silver’s model has Democrats as the favourites to win with a 5–6 point margin in the generic ballot. In the House, Democrats are favourites if they win by 2–3 points.

 Read more:
 The American mood is turning dark, and Republicans are likely to pay the price at the midterms

Democrats lead Republicans by one to four points in polls of Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Alaska and Ohio. Trump won all these states by double-digit margins in 2024. In Nebraska, a Republican is only 0.1 points ahead of an independent. But Democrats are only leading by 2.8 points in Maine, which Kamala Harris won by 6.9 points.

Silver said on Saturday that Democrats lead in polls of 54 Senate races (including seats not up for election). If polls are basically right nationally, Democrats have an 88% chance to win the Senate, with an average of 52.4 senators.

If polls are systematically overstating Democrats by 3–4 points nationally, Democrats’ chance of winning the Senate drops to 38%, with an average of 49.7 senators. But if polls are understating Democrats by 3–4 points nationally, their chance to win the Senate rises to 99% with an average of 54.6 senators.

Economic data

Americans are currently paying an average of US$4.30 a gallon for regular petrol (gasoline in the US), down from US$4.36 a gallon in my October 7 article and US$4.48 on September 25. Owing to profits and taxes, the retail price of petrol will be higher than the commodity price.

The commodity price of petrol had surged from a low of US$2.99 a gallon on August 27 to US$3.59 on September 23, but has fallen back to its current US$3.19 a gallon.

However, the international benchmark Brent oil has surged from US$96.16 a barrel on September 29 to US$109.86 last Friday, the highest it has been since May. There appears to be a lag between changes in oil prices and petrol prices, so petrol prices are likely to increase again before the midterms.

In Silver’s models, Trump and Republicans were at a high in early September, shortly after the August 27 low point in petrol prices.

The September inflation report was released last Wednesday. Owing to high petrol prices, inflation increased 0.6% in September, up from 0.4% in August. Core inflation was up 0.3%, the same as in August. Annual inflation was 3.7%, the highest it has been before the midterms since 1990, except during COVID. Core annual inflation was 2.6%.

Real (inflation-adjusted) wages fell 0.5% in both hourly and weekly terms in September owing to high inflation and low wage growth. Annual real wages were down 0.7% in hourly terms and down 0.1% in weekly terms.

After combined losses of 1.9% in the last three trading sessions, the benchmark US S&P stock market index was down 2.0% last Friday from its October 6 peak. But it was still up 10.3% from its peak in the week before the Iran war began in late February and up 16.2% from its worst point in the Iran war in late March.

Democrat megachurch pastor, Adam Hamilton, has spent his campaign for Senate in Kansas railing against billionaires and special interests, but his financial disclosure shows he has a net worth of up to $20 million and earns a salary more than twice the salary paid to U.S. senators from Church of the Resurrection.

news.title: Black Enthusiasm Gap Haunts Far Left Democrats
news.text:
Throughout the current election cycle, the pundit class has made much of an enthusiasm gap that purportedly bedevils the Republicans. The Democrats, they tell us, are far more motivated to vote in the midterms than are their GOP counterparts. Oddly, we have heard very little about recent polls showing that the gap between extremely motivated Republicans and Democrats has narrowed considerably. Even more puzzling is the absence of any serious commentary on the very real lack of enthusiasm among Black voters for far-left Democratic candidates. Two recipients of this lukewarm Black support are Democratic Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico.

El-Sayed is, of course, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s open seat. He won the nomination by less than a single percentage point in the party’s primary, but his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), handily defeated him by 28 points in the heavily black Detroit area. And the news gets worse. A recent Washington Post-Schar School poll found the following: “Among likely Black voters, 83 percent say they want Democrats to control the Senate but 67 percent back El-Sayed.” And the portentous polling news for the Democrats just keeps on coming: “A Fox News poll conducted in late September found that just 77 percent of African American voters were supportive of El-Sayed, significantly below the usual Democratic benchmark for the demographic.” 

To illustrate exactly how lethal these numbers are for El-Sayed’s campaign against his Republican opponent, former U.S. Congressman Mike Rogers, Vice President Kamala Harris received 89 percent of the Black vote in Michigan during the 2024 presidential election — and still lost the state to Trump. Thus, as many as 15 to 20 percent of them may sit this one out. Why? One participant in an MS Now focus group summed it up succinctly: “I think he’s taking advantage that we as Black people are Democratic, and he think we gonna vote for him anyway. And I’m like, ‘No sir, I’m gonna put uncommitted down on that little circle and move on.’” Meanwhile, Detroit’s second largest newspaper, the Detroit News, firmly refuses to endorse him:

Our gravest concerns involve El-Sayed’s associations with figures who have excused or minimized terrorism, his reluctance to unequivocally condemn dangerous rhetoric, and his support of extreme policies. At a time of rising anti-semitism, Democrats deserve leadership that unequivocally rejects rhetoric threatening Jewish communities … During the Oct. 8 Senate debate, El-Sayed also declined to identify whether Iran or Israel posed the greater threat to America, dismissing the comparison as hypothetical. Such evasiveness is unacceptable given the Iranian regime’s decades-long record of killing Americans, sponsoring terrorism and destabilizing the Middle East. CheckVoting Info

A loss by El-Sayed would substantially reduce the Democratic Party’s chances of winning a Senate majority because the seat is now held by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The Republicans now enjoy a 53-47 majority, and they have the advantage of a GOP vice president who can cast a tie-breaking vote on legislation and presidential appointments. Consequently, in order to retake the Senate, the Democrats must hold every seat they now control, and flip four seats currently held by Republicans. If El-Sayed loses, the net number of Senate seats they need to flip will increase to five. Unless, of course, they manage to flip a Republican seat in some other state. This brings us to the truly weird Democratic nominee for the Senate seat in Texas.

James Talarico defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) for the Democratic Senate nomination last March in a rancorous primary, the result of which was not accepted gracefully by the latter. As the Washington Times reported at the time, “Rep. Jasmine Crockett said this week that her failed bid for the Democratic Senate nomination in Texas was marred by racism, and made clear she does not intend to campaign alongside the man who beat her, state Rep. James Talarico.” He now faces Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the general election, after Mr. Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn in a less than amicable Republican runoff in May. Crockett’s response to Democratic pressure to campaign with Talarico was reported by The Austin Independent:

The best thing that I can do for James Talarico isn’t me standing on a stage with him. It is the fact that I endorsed five candidates in the runoff who all happen to be Black men in the state of Texas and every single one of them won and they’re going on to November, meaning that they will pull out more Black people to vote. People keep trying to say, ‘well, Jasmine has to go and hold his hand.’ Nah, I don’t. And, honestly some people (are) just not gonna be sold on certain people that are running in the state of Texas. So the best thing I can do is take down ballot candidates, who no one’s ever heard of, and do my best to uplift them and increase the voter participation. FollowPolitics

Not only will Rep. Crockett not campaign with him, but Talarico has been blasted by a Black civic group for cancelling a campaign event during his bizarre 12-day disappearance from the campaign trail. According to a Fox News report, the Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium is profoundly frustrated that the Talarico campaign shows no interest in rescheduling the event: “It was a missed opportunity for Representative Talarico to directly address community skepticism and demonstrate the sincerity of his commitment to Central Texas African Americans.” Much of the frustration involved Talarico’s July pledge to spend $25 million on Black voter outreach. Only 2 percent of these funds ever arrived.

All of which brings us to the distrust with which Black voters view the Democratic Party. These voters increasingly believe the Democrats take their votes for granted and that Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico personify that attitude. They are not wrong. If elected, both of these candidates will revert to extreme positions that many Black voters don’t support and will be absent from their communities until the next election rolls. Voters, regardless of race, don’t like to be taken for fools. El-Sayed and Talarico may very well learn that lesson soon.

news.title: Eminem defends Kid Rock team-up amid fans criticism
news.text:
Eminem and Kid Rock may not see eye to eye politically, but their decades-long friendship just landed them on the same track.

The Detroit rappers have reunited for Rock’s new faith-based album, Halfway 2 Jesus, released Friday.

Eminem appears on Heal My Faith, a collaboration that raised eyebrows among fans familiar with his past criticism of Donald Trump and his public endorsement of Kamala Harris at a Detroit rally in 2024.

Slim Shady has now addressed the reaction, making it clear that politics wasn’t the point of the reunion.

“Not about choosing sides, just choosing to make music with my old friend. Praying for all of us.”

Rock also explained the unlikely team-up in an interview with Billboard. Although Eminem was initially announced for another track, 7 Sins, he ultimately appeared on Heal My Faith – the song Rock originally wanted him for. “We agreed we didn’t need two songs together…people are going to think we’re dating,” Rock said.

The rocker said their friendship goes back decades and that he didn’t want to pull Eminem into his political world.

“We’ve been friends for, like, 40 years. I really didn’t want to drag him into my political world….. We talk about [politics] a little bit, not a ton. There’s a lot of stuff we agree on, and we can have a laugh about what [we don’t]. That’s why I asked him to write a verse for me.”

Eminem makes the distinction between friendship and politics clear in his verse, rapping: “From shock rap to the rock rap / My homie and me /He is my brother, not my political enemy,” before delivering a message about faith and unity across political divides.

Rock said the album is intended to promote forgiveness, second chances and a little more grace in a divided country.

This guy's a jihadist.(END VC)MARGARET BRENNAN: Abdul El-Sayed, how is he handling that kind of rhetoric, which is basically accusing him of being a terrorist, and is the Republican candidate comfortable with this?ED O'KEEFE: Well, he's repeating it himself. We saw him give a speech this week just ahead of the vice president on Thursday in the Detroit area where he spent about 90 percent of his speech laying out accusations similar to what the president is suggesting, that he has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, that he's too extreme for Michigan, that he hasn't denounced the IRGC and thinks that Israel's a bigger threat than Iran.El-Sayed has, in various ways, addressed this by saying, first of all, no, he has no associations with the Muslim Brotherhood. He was asked by a voter, does he disavow them? The answer was "yes." It was followed by a long respond targeting that person for raising it at all and suggesting that the only reason Republicans are doing this is because he's Muslim or Arab and is different. He ties himself to the legacies of John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama in being firsts. But the difference was, Kennedy and Obama, I'd argue, went out and sort of proactively addressed the fact that they would be historic and different in speeches.MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.ED O'KEEFE: And did it in a – in a – I guess a more positive way. El- Sayed continues to sort of raise it, or answer questions about it and then accuse people of being – why would you raise that?MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.ED O'KEEFE: Well, he's the one raising it to some extent by pointing out the history of it. But then when people ask these questions, it gets quite defensive and aggressive about it.The thing is, he's anticipating that voters in Michigan are more upset about the economy, more upset about the war, less concerned about him. It is quite the gamble. And one that he continues to say he's going to win by seven percent. I don't think the polls show that. But he's standing by about to win by seven percent. We'll see.MARGARET BRENNAN: Just quickly on Michigan. You interviewed Mike Rogers and you asked him about his wife handing out $10 cards to go buy gas.ED O'KEEFE: Yes. Yes.MARGARET BRENNAN: Is that legal?ED O'KEEFE: Well, buying votes is not legal, no. And I asked Rogers, what was your wife doing there? And he said, well, she paid for these out-of- pocket and she was trying to raise awareness about our campaign.MARGARET BRENNAN: How does that make a difference?ED O'KEEFE: I – that was his answer when I asked, right?MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.ED O'KEEFE: I mean you saw – this was on social media. People caught this. But he also made the point that she was doing this in black areas of Detroit. He has made a concerted effort to reach out to black voters in that city, believing that there is softness for El-Sayed, and the polling suggests there is. And certainly what we heard this week suggests that he still has work to do there. But Rogers is trying to make inroads there. Handing out gift cards, meeting with pastors. He told me at one point that he met a black pastor who, in his 70 years that that church had existed, no Republican office holder or politician had ever shown up.MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.ED O'KEEFE: That might work on the margins in close races. We'll see.MARGARET BRENNAN: Caitlin, you have spent some time in Kansas. President Trump's heading there.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes.MARGARET BRENNAN: We were just talking about beef prices with the North Dakota senator.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes.MARGARET BRENNAN: This is a problem for Roger Marshall in Kansas.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: I mean I was there a couple weeks ago, not a place I expected to be in the final stretch of this campaign. No Democrat has won the Senate race in Kansas since 1932. That's nearly a century.But there's a lot at place here that I think speaks to the broader themes of this election. First of all, kind of going back to the point I made, Roger Marshall is a candidate – a current incumbent that Republicans kind of feel meh about. They like the president, but not necessarily translating to him. Everything you've been seeing across the country, the cost of diesel, especially for farmers in Kansas, is important.But I spent an afternoon with a cattle farmer in Kansas who likes the president, supported the president, time and again, still supports him, but the decision that the administration made to allow beef imports into the market, that is something that is directly affecting him. And he told me, for the first time he is considering voting for the Democrat Adam Hamilton here, who I interviewed, and he said, you know, if you talk to him, he often references that he's a former Republican, he's not campaigning on the national party brand, which he can't do in a place like Kansas.MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: But he's making it competitive because of kind of that perfect storm of complications that Republicans have going for them. And then the nuances in a lot of these races. Administration policies directly affecting the constituencies that tend to vote for Trump. So, that gets to the turnout question.MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Is that enough to depress them and enough to convert a couple of them?MARGARET BRENNAN: And that, Anthony, is what you're going to be focused on basically all night on November 3rd.ANTHONY SALVANTO: Yes. Well, look, this national context, to Caitlin's point, is neither party not only is viewed favorably, but neither one is viewed by most as able to help you financially.MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.ANTHONY SALVANTO: And that's important because, yes, is speaks to localized races or state-specific races, in many cases that Democrats would like this to be all nationalized because, on the national level, there is that opposition to the administration's policies.But, at the same time, when you talk about who owns the economy and you ask that, it is the Trump administration in the minds of most, because of those policies, because of the war, and because of gas prices.MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.Very quickly, Caitlin, any word on who's behind these 36 lawmakers receiving threatening envelopes?CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes, suspicious substances, a lot of them intercepted before they reached Capitol Hill offices. But not only for U.S. senators and lawmakers, but also for election officials, which is really startling. It's been 25 years since the anthrax issue after 9/11. And what is really especially jarring is, they don't – they haven't released who – or talked about who may be behind this. Federal law enforcement is investigating. But the uptick that we've seen and threats against lawmakers and their families has risen in the past year over 50 percent.MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Yes, it's something we are tracking very much in our public life these days.Thank you all for this panel.ED O'KEEFE: Good to see you.MARGARET BRENNAN: Get ready, it's going to be a fun two weeks.CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Buckle up.MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be back in a moment.(ANNOUNCEMENTS)MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. We'll see you next week.(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

news.title: The 'cowardly' truth exposed as Republicans run and hide from critics
news.text:
A growing number of Republicans are declining to take part in debates against their midterm opponents, and as one campaign communications veteran wrote for MS NOW, there is a "cowardly" truth that they are actually hiding from.

Symone Sanders-Townsend is an MS NOW host and contributor who also previously worked as a political strategist and national press secretary for Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign, as well as a White House spokesperson and senior advisor for former Vice President Kamala Harris. In a new piece published Sunday morning, she detailed the growing trend of Republicans ducking out of planned debates against their Democratic opponents.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, she noted, has taken part in election debates throughout his time in politics. Now, however, as polls show his current opponent, Gina Hinojosa, gaining on him, he suddenly "decided a debate is unnecessary," prompting Hinojosa to hold an event outside the governor's mansion. Elsewhere in Texas, GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton has declined to debate his increasingly popular opponent, James Talarico.

"In Florida, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody has declined to debate Angie Nixon," Sanders-Townsend wrote. "In Mississippi, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith said there’s 'no point' in debating Democratic nominee Scott Colom. Why are so many Republicans making the same decision in the same election cycle?... I have some thoughts."

Sanders-Townsend highlighted her own past experience working as "deputy communications director for the Democratic nominee for governor in Nebraska" in the 2014 midterms, which she said were anything but a "pleasant" time to be a Democratic candidate. Republicans had successfully turned President Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act into a heated political issue, making it "difficult to keep the conversation focused on the issues we wanted to discuss" when the conversation would invariably get wrenched towards taking Democrats to task for the ACA.

Now, the tables are turned, she argued, and Republicans are running scared at the prospect of having to answer for their capitulation to President Donald Trump and his toxic agenda.

"That is the political environment I recognize today, except Republicans are now being asked to defend the president’s agenda," Sanders-Townsend wrote. "Donald Trump unilaterally imposed tariffs, raising costs for American businesses and consumers. Then came his war of choice in Iran. Gas and diesel prices climbed, raising costs for households and businesses. And Americans are still waiting for a clear explanation of how this war will end. Where were Republicans in Congress?"

She added later: "A debate means explaining those choices — or why you didn’t challenge them — while someone a few feet away questions your answer. I can understand why a campaign might not want that. But refusing to face those questions is cowardly... A politician who treats difficult questions as optional is telling us how they understand the power they hold. Perhaps the most revealing thing about these Republicans isn’t what they might say on a debate stage. It’s what they believe they no longer have to explain."

news.title: Bernie Sanders admits Democrats failed working-class voters on economics, driving them to Donald Trump
news.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., acknowledged on Saturday that Democrats failed working-class Americans economically, contributing to voters abandoning the party for President Donald Trump. When asked during an interview on MS NOW what exactly Democrats had done wrong to lose working-class voters to Trump, Sanders pointed to the party's economic record, arguing that its failure to address their financial struggles had contributed to declining support. "What I think what Trump did, again — this gets back to my view — that the Democratic Party failed working-class people on economic issues," Sanders said. "I think they have a lot to be proud of in terms of fighting for civil rights, for women's rights, for gay rights, for environmental stuff, but in terms of working-class issues, no, I don't think they've done a good job," he added. JAMES CARVILLE BLAMES BERNIE SANDERS FOR TRUMP BEING PRESIDENT IN FIERY RANT Sanders, an independent, pointed to unfulfilled economic promises and trade agreements he blamed for the loss of American manufacturing jobs as reasons working-class voters became disillusioned with the party. "What they did is for years, they heard the Democrats say, 'Oh, we're going to do this, we're going to do that, and we're going to help you.' And they didn't. And it's true. Democrats pushed through terrible trade deals, which cost us millions of good-paying manufacturing jobs, et cetera, et cetera. They lost faith in the Democratic Party, and not unjustifiably. All right?" Sanders said. When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Republican National Committee national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre criticized Democrats' economic policies and argued that the party had abandoned working families. DEMOCRATS PUNISH MEMBERS WHO PUT WORKING AMERICANS AHEAD OF PARTY LOYALTY "Democrats can no longer claim to be the working class party when they hammer Americans with higher taxes, ship jobs overseas, and kill off the industries that make our country thrive. Democrats' only interest is appeasing their far-left base that wants to destroy our country from the inside out, and working families pay the price." A 2024 Fox News Voter Analysis found that Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris 53% to 45% among voters with household incomes between $50,000 and $99,999. Harris carried voters earning $100,000 or more by 53% to 46%. Trump also won voters who reported falling behind financially by 29 percentage points, while around 40% of voters identified inflation as the most important factor in their vote, a group that backed Trump by nearly a two-to-one margin. This isn't the first time Sanders has called out the Democratic Party for abandoning the working class. Following Trump's 2024 presidential victory, Sanders excoriated the Democratic Party. TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK "It should come as no great surprise that a Democratic Party which has abandoned working-class people would find that the working class has abandoned them. First, it was the white working class, and now it is Latino and Black workers as well," Sanders said in the statement. "While the Democratic leadership defends the status quo, the American people are angry and want change. And they're right," he continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APPRep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who also appeared in the special, emphasized the growing importance of economic class in American politics and defended Sanders' approach to working-class issues. "As the gap between the rich and the working class get bigger and bigger, and as the middle class, or our understanding of the middle class, starts to really disappear in this country, and more and more people that had previously felt okay find themselves more squeezed than ever," she said. "I think that this has allowed the salience of class to really emerge in our politics." news.title: Midterm vote is about 'what's best for my family': Voters talk 2026 midterms
news.text:
Josh York, a retired Army major who now works in health care administration in Anchorage, Alaska, has seen firsthand how high prices for fuel have kept Alaskans off the road. In the far reaches of America’s largest state, prices are as high as $24 per gallon.

“The gas prices don't seem to be coming down, and believe me, I watch,” York, a three-time Trump voter, told ABC News.

“Recently, we were out in the middle of rural Alaska, and we were paying $8.99 a gallon for gas,” York said, blaming the higher prices on the Iran war. That war has substantially slowed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited before the war.

The economy is on Americans’ minds across the country ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3, when voters in a handful of key states will wield outsize impact on control of the United States Congress.

ABC News traveled to those states -- Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire, and Maine -- finding many Americans who are frustrated with their personal finances and aware their vote would be a referendum on President Donald Trump’s job performance.

The Frontier state

Trump traveled outside the continental United States this week to boost Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who faces a reelection challenge from Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola – one of four seats the Democrats hope they can capture to win control of the U.S. Senate.

The president defended the war against Iran, telling Alaskans the war would end soon and prices would come down when it did, and said his opponents had made the election about affordability.

“Every time they want to try and get me, they say 'affordability, sir. This and that.' I said, 'They caused the problem,’ he said at a rally in Wasilla, 45 miles north of Anchorage. “But we have reduced it very substantially.’”

The Senate race – analyzed as a toss-up in a state where Trump won by 13 points in 2024 – is reflecting the price pressures of voters. 

The president’s polling numbers have plummeted to record lows in recent months. Just over half of Americans, 52%, strongly disapprove of Trump, according to a new ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll.

Sullivan, who is aligned with Trump and has backed the Iran war, acknowledged the conflict was causing higher prices and said it should end “soon.”

One voter said heating costs in Fairbanks had even exceeded mortgage costs.

York told ABC News’ Martha Raddatz, co-anchor of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos," that even though he’s voted for Trump, he disapproved of the president across the board: in his handling of the economy, the Iran war and the overall direction the president was taking the country.

York, unsure about his decision between the candidates, said his vote would come down to the economy.

“I know that they both have their ideas for Alaska and how they want to do things. And I'm not gonna say one's right versus the other being wrong,” he said. “But at this point, I've got to look at what's best for my family. I've got to look at what's best for my kids.”

The heartland

In America’s heartland, voters told ABC News energy prices and the president’s trade policy were animating discussions around the midterm elections, including in a competitive Iowa senate race.

The rising diesel prices have crunched farmers who rely on diesel for transport.

“Our tanks over there hold 3,500 gallons. It costs $20,000 now to fill them. A year ago it cost [about] $12,000,” said cattle farmer Dan Pederson, who voted for the president three times.

“The ripple effect – hauling cattle, pickups, trucks, everything [is] just-- it's just astronomical. It's crazy,” he said.

Pederson said among his “staunch Republican friends” there was a lot of “wavering” on Trump. The Republican candidate for the Senate seat, Rep. Ashley Hinson, has broken with the president, urging him to bring the Iran war to an end.

The president announced an extraordinary remedy to the price of diesel last week, saying in a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin that the two leaders had agreed to a “diesel deal” that would allow Russian diesel, largely blocked by sanctions and trapped because of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, to enter world markets.

Many Republican lawmakers said the president’s move would benefit an autocratic government that invaded its neighbor, Ukraine.

“We need to lower gas prices in this country,” Hinson said. “We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.”

In neighboring Nebraska, Republican congressman Don Bacon, who is stepping away from his own seat, said Republicans’ formula of backing Trump could prove costly.

The Republican worries about his party’s odds in traditionally red Nebraska and Kansas, midwestern Senate races where Democrats hope to manage surprise victories, he told Raddatz.

He credited his own independent streak with his own election victories.

“You got to be able to show that you're your own person and you represent the district,” he said.

In an X post this week, Bacon said Trump’s deal with Putin was a betrayal of Ukraine.

The president was “propping up a dictator’s invasion and throwing an ally under the bus,” he wrote. 

The independent Northeast

In the country’s Northeast, independent voters wield considerable influence. 

Democratic-leaning states here have continued to elect Republicans – like Maine’s five-term Sen. Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth election.

Collins is one of the few Senate Republicans who regularly breaks with Trump, saying in a recent debate she “voted nine times against the president on the Iran war.”

Voters pointed to her role as the top appropriator in Congress, overseeing the key funding mechanisms that Mainers say gives them a crucial voice in Washington.

In a polarized era, voters said it’s Collins’ independent brand that has won her respect.

“I think that objectively speaking, she is the most bipartisan member of the Senate, and I think we need more Susan Collins, not fewer,” said self-described life-long Democrat Mary Anne Lynch. She plans to cast her ballot for Collins this November.

Brenda Garrand has been in Collins’ camp before, voting for her three times – but she says she won’t in 2026.

“I would say, for me, the most important reason to vote for Troy Jackson is to make sure that there is a Democratic Senate,” Garrand said.

Collins was not doing enough with her powerful perch, she argued.

“She has gone a step too far … [I’m] deeply disappointed in her behavior as a woman who has really reached the apex of an ability to make a difference,” Garrand said.

The Democratic senate nominee in neighboring New Hampshire sees the same dynamics at play in his state. Congressman Chris Pappas told Raddatz that Democrats’ margins in the Granite State had improved since Vice President Kamala Harris’s narrow victory there in 2024.

“I'm meeting Republicans every day that are opposed to what they see this administration doing,” he said. “I'm meeting libertarian-minded voters in the ‘Live Free or Die’ state that don't support the disgraceful immigration overreach with respect to [Immigrations and Custom Enforcement.]”

Pappas faces a known name brand in New Hampshire politics: John Sununu, the brother of Republican Gov. Chris Sununu.

Chris Ager, a former chair of the New Hampshire Republican party, called Sununu “that quintessential New Hampshire politician – very pragmatic, very common sense, very independent of Washington.”

He added, “I think that's going to sell very well on Nov. 3.”
news.summary: ABC News spoke with voters in Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire and Maine.
news.author: Chris Boccia,Julia Cherner,Tommy Brooksbank

news.title: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. What's their next move?
news.text: CASA GRANDE: Chris Martinez feels like Donald Trump has made a fool of him. The 28-year-old maintenance technician from Casa Grande, Arizona, voted for the Republican president expecting to get a thriving economy and no wars.Instead, gas prices are so high that Martinez returned one of his vehicles to the lender, he shifted his food shopping to a discount grocer and he has watched as the United States has spent months in conflict with Iran."He's doing nothing for us, to benefit us," Martinez said, adding, "I got duped and I feel like a dummy."As a group, Latinos shifted toward Trump two years ago, helping return him to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress. Now, many like Martinez are souring on the president and his party.The path to a US House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, Colorado and Texas, where Democrats are counting on disaffected Trump supporters to swing back their way. It is unclear whether Democrats have sealed the deal with voters who lack strong allegiance to either party.An Arizona farming town faces a transitionCasa Grande, the town of 70,000, sits at a crossroads between Phoenix and Tucson. There is a quaint downtown surrounded by master-planned developments offering affordable housing for people priced out of larger cities. Gated golf-course communities attract retirees.Much of the town is at the northern tip of Arizona's 6th Congressional District. Republican Juan Ciscomani is seeking a third term. Two years ago, Ciscomani won by 2.5 percentage points and Trump won by less than 1 point.This time, Ciscomani is subtly creating distance from Trump. The congressman talks up his immigrant story — he was born in Mexico and moved to the US as a kid — and frames himself as independent and bipartisan.Ciscomani's Democratic opponent is JoAnna Mendoza. The former Marine emphasizes her own hardscrabble upbringing as the daughter of immigrant farmworkers who worked the fields close to Casa Grande."People trust you if they know that you came from the community and understand their way of life," Mendoza said in an interview earlier this year..Analysis: For Trump, results have often revealed the art of 'no deal'.Most Hispanic voters disapprove of TrumpTrump made broad gains among Hispanics during the 2024 campaign.Now, about 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. More than 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.Their potential shift away from Republicans this year would be driven by anti-Trump sentiment, not a love of Democrats, said Mike Madrid, a political consultant who wrote "The Latino Century," a book about Latino voters, and co-hosts "The Latino Vote" podcast.Latinos are in the midst of a "dealignment," rejecting strong associations with both parties because neither is speaking effectively to working class economic concerns, he said.Hispanics are about evenly split on their view of the Democratic Party, according to the October AP-NORC poll. Their views of the Republican Party are more negative, with 55% having an unfavorable view and 38% having a favorable one.The economy is at the center of a Colorado contestOn a recent morning in Denver, Democratic state lawmaker Manny Rutinel stood before a crowd of union carpenters and rolled up his sleeve to show off a scar from when he sold his blood more than 100 times to make ends meet."I'm the son of a single mom. She came to America to give me the American Dream. We worked hard for this country," Rutinel said.Rutinel is challenging Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th Congressional District, which stretches from blue-collar Denver suburbs to energy-rich farm and ranchland in the northern part of the state. Latinos are the district's single largest ethnic group, and both the incumbent and challenger are Hispanic. Evans won by less than 1 percentage point while Trump won by 2 points.Rutinel has focused relentlessly on the economy. Evans, a 40-year-old former police lieutenant, has portrayed Rutinel as having a record as a left-wing activist and liberal lawmaker..'Way too far': Latino Trump voters shocked by Minneapolis immigration crackdown.Jose Montalvo, a 47-year-old trucker, voted for Evans even though he supported Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024. He likes to split his ticket between the parties but does not think he will do that this year. Montalvo is frustrated by Trump's handling of gas prices, saying "I blame him for the fuel side of things." That is a criticism he extends to all Republicans.Maria del Carmen Rojas, a naturalized citizen who has lived in the United States for 36 years, said she is shocked that any Latinos could back Trump and a Republican Party that she thinks regularly denigrates immigrants."We Latinos contribute very much to this country, the taxes we pay, the service we provide," she said.Frustration mounts in Texas' Rio Grande ValleyA wooden sign that said "need prayer?" sat on a table with free Bibles along a busy suburban walking trail in Edinburg, Texas, on a hot October evening.The town is part of the state's 15th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 18 points but is now viewed as a top Election Day battleground.Standing behind the table, Thomas Centrella, 42, said he has grown disillusioned with politics. He doubts he would ever vote for a Democrat but said he might skip elections or turn independent in the future.Maria Elsa Gonzalez, who is retired, said she will again support the district's Republican congresswoman, Monica de la Cruz, instead of Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star. Speaking in Spanish, Gonzalez said Pulido "doesn't have any preparation other than a pretty face and the fame of singing pretty."Priscilla Olivarez, 46, a public education teacher, is undecided in the midterms. She grew up as a Democrat and voted Republican in the last presidential election. Today, she is disappointed with an economy where costs seem to be growing faster than wages and she often digs into her own pocket to help pay for things in the classroom. "I stand independent right now because I don't agree with either side right now," she said..Economic frustration tests Trump's standing with US rural voters, new AP-KFF poll finds.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
